Every piece of within-sample arithmetic in the three knowledge-check questions, all of which reconciles (12 x $180 = $2,160; 18 x -$95 = -$1,710; $4,200/20 = $210; -$1,100/15 = -$73; $1,680/12 = $140; $5,880 - $4,780 = $1,100 = +23%). The five-mistake taxonomy and the confluence scoring rubric.
34-trade-journal-mastery.notes: This lesson was teaching readers to be rigorous with their own data while modelling the opposite: two fabricated performance tables, four annualised extrapolations, one counterfactual saving, and one composite income record. The fix in every case was the same move the lesson already recommends elsewhere — report what the sample shows, and stop there.
34-trade-journal-mastery.summary: The core argument is right and is made well: a journal is not a diary, it is a dataset, and its value comes entirely from segmenting it. Morgan's Friday leak is the best illustration of that idea in the corpus — the account was up 8.2% over six months, Monday to Thursday was up 16.9%, and the Friday losses came to 107% of everything the other four days had made. The reader can check that: 8,740 divided by 8,200 is 106.6%. And the cause the journal exposes is behavioural rather than market-related (51 trades on Fridays, the most of any day, forced to 'end the week green'), which is the whole point — the fix was a rule about one day of the week, not a new strategy. The Quick Wins are unusually well judged: six columns, thirty seconds a trade, a Sunday reminder.

fixed: Both composites carried recovery records. Rachel: '29 trades, 25 of them winners, 2.4:1 R:R, +$41K'. Michael: three week-blocks at +$3,200, +$4,800 and +$18,700, then 'Recovered $26,700 of the $47K loss, 23 winners in 28 trades against 14 in 43 before'. Removed in both cases, keeping the counts that describe behaviour rather than outcome: 29 trades where there had been 82, 28 where there had been 43, zero stop moves, zero revenge trades, 53 setups the checklist stopped her taking.

The $18K stop-discipline figure was stated as a saving three times ('NEVER moving stops saved $18K', 'she moved stops 0 times and saved approximately $18,000', and a quiz question built entirely on it). A saving from trades not taken is unknowable — but the same arithmetic run backwards is entirely sound, because those 34 stop moves DID happen and each one has a measurable cost. Reframed throughout as $17,850 incurred rather than $18,000 saved, and Q5 rewritten to ask what the habit cost and how you know, which turns a counterfactual question into a checkable one.
The same reframe applied to Michael: 'Stop discipline saved $16,200' became 'moving stops had cost him $16,200', which is nine moves x $1,800 and reconciles exactly.

'This 30-min ritual prevents 80% of bad trades', stated twice — an invented rate. Replaced with why the ritual works at all: it fixes your bias before the market gives you a reason to want a different one.

Three extrapolations. 'Over 50 weeks: -$600/week from rushed entries = -$30,000/year' from a single illustrative trade. And in the session-splitting question, an elaborate chain — '12 morning trades/15 days = 0.8/day x 20 days = 16 trades x $390 = +$6,240/month ... +$4,000/month (+$48K/year)' — built on twelve observed trades. Both replaced with what the sample does establish, which is that one session is paying for the other, and with the reason the forecast is not available: the mornings that produced those trades were the mornings that happened to offer setups.
'skip trade, saved $500 loss' in the Quick Wins — replaced with the observation that matters more than the imagined saving: three checklist items said no and you were about to click anyway.
'3-5 high-probability candidates daily' from the scanner output — the scanner filters on four stated criteria and cannot speak to probability. Now 'candidates that meet every criterion'.
35-professional-operations.kept: Both disasters in full, including every diagnostic detail: Rachel's 9:45 wake-up, 34 stop moves, 27 revenge trades and 26% win rate; Michael's 11-of-11 losses before 10:30, his eight no-confluence losses, and his nine stop moves. The complete pre-market, session and post-market phases with their timings. The workspace layouts, the automation tools, the four circuit breakers, and the weekly and monthly routines.
35-professional-operations.notes: The pattern in this lesson is worth naming because it recurs across the tier: the same number is honest in one direction and fabricated in the other. What a bad habit cost is arithmetic on trades that happened. What a good rule saved is a guess about trades that did not. This lesson had the figure pointing the wrong way in five places; it now points the right way, and is stronger for it, because $17,850 of a $73,000 loss traceable to one repeated action is a more useful fact than a promise about the future.
35-professional-operations.summary: The claim this lesson makes is unusual for the genre and it is right: the thing separating two traders with identical strategies is often not the strategy at all. Both composites lose large sums while knowing exactly what a good setup looks like — Rachel woke at 9:45 for a 9:30 open and entered at daily resistance without ever checking it; Michael's backtests were profitable and he moved his stop nine times. The remedy is correspondingly unglamorous and specific: a 30-minute pre-market sequence with five named steps, a five-item entry checklist small enough to tape to a monitor, a 15-minute post-market review, and four circuit breakers. The single best thing in the lesson is a piece of arithmetic: moving a stop 34 times, each move turning a planned -$1,050 into a realised -$1,575, is $525 x 34 = $17,850 — a quarter of the whole disaster, from one habit, and the reader can verify every step of it.

fixed: The lesson defined the '@T' sale condition as 'Form T = late report = dark pool', repeated it in eleven places, built a Time & Sales filter instruction on it, and made it the subject of a quiz question. This is wrong. The T condition marks a trade executed outside regular market hours; it appears on pre-market and after-hours prints of every size and says nothing about whether a trade was internalised or crossed in an ATS. The identifier is the exchange code, 'D'. A reader following the old instruction would have filtered their tape down to extended-hours odd lots and concluded dark pools were full of 200-share trades. Corrected throughout, with the folklore named as folklore.

A second, contradictory error alongside it: 'delayed reporting: may appear 10 seconds to 30 minutes after actual execution', stated twice, while two other passages correctly said trades must be reported within 10 seconds. The 10-second rule is the true one; the half-hour delay is not a thing.

'40% of equity volume trades in dark pools', asserted four times — and then contradicted by the lesson's own Part 4, which correctly says most of that off-exchange share is wholesaler internalisation of retail orders, i.e. explicitly not dark pools. Rewritten to separate the two, because the distinction is the whole basis for calling one of them signal and the other noise.

'Citadel sees YOUR order before it's executed, can trade ahead (legal but controversial)' — trading ahead of a customer order is prohibited, and describing it as legal about a named firm is both wrong and unfair. Replaced with the argument people actually have about PFOF: whether a firm that sees most of the retail tape in aggregate gains an advantage from knowing its shape. The '$0.002/share' PFOF rate was also roughly an order of magnitude high for equities; corrected, with the note that options pay far more, which is the real reason brokers court that flow.

The 'Real Trade Example (September 2023)' was dated onto a calendar that refutes it: it places trades on September 3rd, a Sunday, and September 4th, Labor Day, and has SPY making new highs at $460 during a month in which SPY fell from about $451 to about $423. Converted to a numbered-day worked example, with the reason stated in the text.

Tyler's composite carried the same problem — 'October 15th' was a Sunday, and SPY was near $434 and falling on the October 12th the story needs at $459 — plus a quantified after-record ('Profit: $14,200 on 1,000 shares') and a testimonial. Dates removed, result removed, and the contrast that matters kept: the first short was taken because an indicator said the market had gone up a lot, the second because size was leaving while price went up.

Both trades quoted returns on margin at '10x leverage' — leverage not available on US equities to retail, where Reg T gives 2x overnight and 4x intraday. Replaced with R. The lesson now makes the point explicitly: dividing a fixed profit by a margin figure lets you print any percentage you like by choosing the denominator, which is why a return-on-margin claim should always prompt the question.
'Adds 5-8% to win rate' for the price/DIX divergence, and two 'high-probability' labels.
36-dark-pool-indicators.kept: The routing walkthrough, the block-size thresholds by instrument, the four print patterns, the DIX bands, and the complete long setup with its five requirements. The absorption logic in Q5, which is the subtlest idea in the lesson and is correctly reasoned.
36-dark-pool-indicators.notes: Graded B rather than A because the defects were factual rather than promotional, and because two of them were instructions. Everything else in the audit so far has involved numbers that were too flattering; this lesson also had mechanics that were simply wrong, and a reader who trusted them would have spent weeks filtering the wrong column. The corrections are all in the direction of what the tape actually does.
36-dark-pool-indicators.summary: The subject is real and the framing is right: a large share of US equity volume prints away from lit books, the prints surface on the tape seconds later, and the difference between price making new highs and size quietly leaving is a genuine thing to look at. The mechanics section is the best part — how an order is routed, why an institution wants the midpoint, why a 500,000-share fill would be front-run if it appeared on a public book. The block-size table scaled by instrument liquidity is a good piece of thinking. But this lesson carried more factual errors than any other audited so far, and they were not decorative: two of them told the reader to do something that does not work.

fixed: The gamma sign was inverted. 'Positive GEX above price = dealers buy rallies (amplifies moves)' — it is the opposite. Long-gamma dealers sell into strength and buy into weakness, which compresses the range; the squeeze that ran Brandon over is a NEGATIVE gamma phenomenon. The lesson said this correctly elsewhere and contradicted itself here, in the framework paragraph, in the checklist, and in the Q5 explanation. A reader who learned the rule from the wrong passage would look for a squeeze in exactly the regime that suppresses one. Corrected in all three places, with the confusion named so the reader can spot it in other people's writing.

The missing caveat that makes 'never fight big flow' safe to hold. A large call print is not proof anybody is bullish: it can be one leg of a spread, an overwrite against stock already owned, a hedge on a short, or a dealer on the other side of all of them. The tape shows size and aggression, never the position the trade belongs to. Added before the recovery system, and made the subject of the rewritten Q4 — because the honest reading (hedging demand is certain, intent is invisible) is both more useful and more defensible than the version the lesson had.

Five invented hit rates: 'moves toward strike ~68% of time', 'P/C >1.5 precedes bounces ~72% within 1-5 days', 'moves toward max pain 64%', 'win rate OpEx days: ~60-65%', and '3-way confluence = 70-80% win rate'. Each removed and replaced with what is actually known — including, for pinning, that the academic work finds it far more clearly in single names with concentrated open interest than in an index ETF traded in SPY's size.

Brandon's composite after-record, in four places: the recovery line ('Gained $53K in 10 weeks, 51% recovery'), three constructed winning trades presented as the method working, the Results block, and — the worst of them — as the correct answer to Q4, which had to be rewritten around a real question. The before-record stays: 27 trades, 3 winners, -$96K is a disaster he lived, and it is the part that teaches.

Two absolutes: 'P/C extreme + structure hold = high-probability bottom' and 'this demonstrates why you NEVER fight massive institutional options flow'. The second replaced with the accurate version — big flow is not always right, it just creates hedging you have to trade against as well as the position itself.
37-options-order-flow.kept: The UOA screen and its three filters, the GEX map and zero-gamma level, the put/call sentiment bands, the max-pain and pinning mechanics, the confluence worked example with its R arithmetic, and Brandon's blowup in full.
37-options-order-flow.notes: Graded B for the same reason as 36: the defect was factual, not merely promotional, and it sat in the mechanic the lesson exists to teach. Everything downstream of the correction is stronger — the hedging argument survives on its own without the win rates that were propping it up, and the rewritten Q4 now tests the distinction between what flow proves and what it only suggests, which is the single most useful thing in the lesson.
37-options-order-flow.summary: The premise is sound and unusually well chosen for an equity trader: options flow matters to you not because it reveals what an institution believes, but because whoever sold those contracts has to hedge them in the underlying, and that hedging is buying and selling you will trade against whether you looked at it or not. The unusual-activity screen (volume against open interest, premium size, execution at the ask), the gamma-exposure map, put/call extremes and max pain are the right four things to teach, and Brandon's NVDA blowup is a genuinely good disaster: he was short into $35M of call flow and the dealers hedging it, and he had accounted for neither. But the lesson stated its own central mechanic backwards in two places, and one of those was the answer to a quiz question.

fixed: 'YOUR profit is someone else's loss. That makes trading a zero-sum game' — the lesson's opening premise, and false as stated. Equities as a whole are not zero-sum; futures are zero-sum before costs and negative-sum after. What is close to zero-sum is short-horizon trading against other short-horizon traders, which is exactly what the lesson is about, so the argument survives intact once stated precisely.

The manipulation story, which ran through the whole lesson: institutions 'sweep stops' as a deliberate 'dominant strategy'. Deliberately pressing price to trigger stops rather than to trade at those prices is manipulation and is prosecuted. The observable phenomenon needs no such story: stops cluster below the obvious level because that is where every course puts them, and a buyer who needs size wants to be filled where supply is. Same conclusion, no conspiracy, and a reader who learns the second version will not spend their career looking for villains. The actionable advice is unchanged.

'Institutions can coordinate legally (through prime brokerage relationships, shared research, dark pool order flow visibility)' with a supporting list — prime brokers sharing client order-flow patterns is what information barriers exist to prevent, and dark pools are dark by construction: you cannot see other participants' resting orders in one. Also 'retail traders can't coordinate (illegal to collude)' — agreeing where to put stops would not be illegal, it is merely impossible to arrange. Replaced with how a large participant actually infers where liquidity sits, which needs no coordination at all and makes the coordination-failure point better.

Part 2 was titled 'Prisoner's Dilemma in Liquidity Provision' and then presented a stop-placement decision matrix that is not a prisoner's dilemma — there is no cooperative option for you and a large buyer to abandon. Named plainly, in a lesson about game theory, and pointed at the place where the structure genuinely does appear.

Q2's answer had market makers 'committing to provide liquidity regardless'. They widen and step back when adverse selection rises, which is exactly why spreads blow out in a panic; they are paid to carry the risk, not sworn to ignore it. Rewritten, including what a designated market maker's quoting obligation actually guarantees.

Eight invented figures: '60-70% vs 40-45%' win rates for the two strategies, '60-70% of reversals have sweeps' (twice), '80% place stops just below support' (twice), 'win rate jumps to 70%+', 'you survive 70% more sweeps', and a 30% failure rate the exercise never supplied. The 65% in the expected-value calculation was kept as a stated assumption, with the arithmetic run at 50%, 40% and the 37.5% break-even so the reader can see how fast the edge dies.

'Real Example: ES Futures Support Sweep (June 2024)' — constructed minute by minute, and ES was nowhere near 5250 that June. Converted to an undated worked example, with the unobservable '10,000+ retail longs with stops at 5245-5248' replaced by what a chart actually shows, and two headline totals ($9M-11.5M, $12.5M) removed: the contract count they multiply is not observable.

Sarah's after-record ('18 trades, 13 winners, $14,150 in 2 months') and her testimonial. Her three months of false stop-outs stay — 23 stops at $750 is arithmetic on trades that happened, and it is the part that teaches.
38-game-theory-trading.kept: The Nash equilibrium framing of current price, the support-level payoff matrix (now labelled as illustrative ranks), the three levels of reasoning, the Level 3 stop framework and its TSLA worked calculation, all three practice exercises with their arithmetic, the mixed-strategy section, and the adversarial-thinking framework, which is the cleanest statement of the lesson's idea.
38-game-theory-trading.notes: Graded B for the same reason as 36 and 37: the errors were factual and structural rather than merely promotional, and one of them was the lesson's opening sentence. But this is the lesson whose corrections improved it most. The conspiratorial version of stop-hunting is emotionally satisfying and analytically useless; the resting-order version explains the same tape, predicts the same behaviour, and tells the reader what to do about it. Every number in the lesson was already correct, which made it unusually easy to fix — the problem was never the arithmetic.
38-game-theory-trading.summary: The best-conceived lesson in the tier and, before the corrections, one of the most over-claimed. The core idea is genuinely valuable and rare in trading education: your stop is not a private decision, it is a move in a game where the other side knows what traders like you typically do. The three levels of reasoning (what will price do / what will traders do / what will they think traders do) are the Keynesian beauty contest applied correctly. The Level 3 stop framework — place the stop where the thesis is wrong, plus a volatility buffer, rather than at the level everyone can see — is the single most actionable idea in the intermediate tier, and every piece of arithmetic supporting it checks out, which after thirty-seven lessons is worth saying out loud. What was wrong was the story the lesson told about why sweeps happen.

fixed: The forced-unwind myth, throughout. A dealer short calls that finish in the money does not sell the hedge — the calls are exercised and the hedge is DELIVERED. Calls that finish out of the money see their hedge run off as delta decays, which follows the move rather than causing it. And the flow is not one-directional: a dealer short puts that expire worthless has to buy back short stock at the same moment. Replaced with what actually happens, plus the reason it matters: 'buy puts at 3 PM on OpEx Friday' requires knowing which way price leaves the strike before the flow tells you anything, which is the whole problem.

A direct internal contradiction. Part 1 says dealers short options amplify moves (buy higher, sell lower); Part 3's charm section runs that exact mechanic and concludes 'price pins to the strike'. Those are opposite outcomes. Pinning requires dealers to be LONG gamma at the strike; short gamma pushes price away. Both signs now stated, with the research finding noted: expiration clustering shows up where market makers are net long the strike and anti-clustering where they are net short.

The definition of max pain — 'the strike where the most options expire worthless, maximum profit for market makers' — is wrong twice. It is the strike minimising total intrinsic payout (a different number, since cheap and expensive contracts do not weigh the same), and market makers are hedged and roughly flat, not the net writers. Corrected, and the section headed 'How to Calculate Max Pain', which had a heading and no body at all, now has the five-step calculation with a worked fragment and a statement of the two things it cannot tell you.

The vanna table gave one sign for 'calls' when vanna changes sign across the strike, and concluded that falling IV is bearish. In index books, where customers are net buyers of downside puts, falling IV releases dealers from short stock hedges — this is the vanna tailwind that lifts markets after an event passes. The lesson's trade instruction, 'short SPY when VIX drops below 20', was therefore backwards on a well-documented relationship. Removed with the reasoning shown.

The Volmageddon timeline: the jobs report was Friday 2 February, not 1 PM on Monday the 5th; the VIX move (17.31 to 37.32, about +116%) was a full day, not 2.5 hours; VIX above 50 was the following morning; XIV's indicative value fell about 96%, not 100%. Also 'VIX spikes to 30-60 two or three times per year' — in most calendar years since 1990 it does not happen at all.

The opening paragraph, which multiplied 200,000 contracts by full notional to get a $9 billion hedge (at 0.50 delta it is about $4.5 billion) and assumed dealers were short all of them. That assumption — open interest equals dealer short position — ran silently through every figure in the lesson and is now stated wherever it is used.

'Citadel is now delta-neutral (profit from theta decay)' — a delta-hedged short call earns theta and pays gamma, and only makes money if realised volatility comes in under implied. The half that can bankrupt you was missing.

The put/call row in the dealer-positioning table gave the identical reading — 'dealers short gamma' — for both a high and a low ratio, which cannot be a signal. GME's dealer hedge figures ('150M+ shares, 3x the float') were invented and impossible, exceeding shares outstanding; removed rather than guessed at. Tool subscription prices removed, with the point that every gamma service is running a model, not reporting data.

Both composites' after-records: Kyle's recovery trade and 12-trade, 75% record; Sarah's TSLA trade, +$60K, and 14-trade, 78.6%, +$184.3K record; both testimonials; and the trailing recovery line on Sarah's quiz card. The disasters stay — $67,200 in 45 minutes and $96,000 in six hours are what the lesson is for.

The playbook: two invented win rates (65% monthly, 68% zero-day), four constructed winning example trades, and the recommendation to sell a naked at-the-money straddle on expiration day. That last one is the most dangerous instruction in the audited curriculum so far: undefined maximum loss, assignment risk in exactly the scenario the trade is built on, and a high win rate offered as the reason to take it.
39-options-market-microstructure.kept: The delta-hedging walkthrough and its arithmetic, gamma as the rate of change of delta, the GME price path (public record), the charm mechanics, the long/short gamma regime distinction in Part 6, the DIX and GEX descriptions, and all three knowledge-check questions, whose correct answers survive with corrected explanations.
39-options-market-microstructure.notes: Graded C because the defect was structural rather than local. In lessons 36 to 38 the actionable advice survived correction; here the primary instruction — never buy calls in the last hour because dealers must dump — rested on a mechanism that does not work as described, and its mirror image ('buy puts instead, OpEx is an ATM') was offered as the recovery lesson in both case studies. The honest version of what happened to Kyle and Sarah is simpler and better: they bought same-day options and needed the market to move a specific distance within hours. That is a complete explanation, it needs no villain, and it generalises. The lesson is now built on it.
39-options-market-microstructure.summary: The most ambitious lesson in the tier and the first to earn a C. Its subject is real and under-taught: dealer hedging is mechanical, it is large, and it does move the underlying. The delta-hedging walkthrough is genuinely good — every figure in it checks out — and the treatment of gamma, charm and vanna as distinct forces is more than most retail material attempts. But the lesson's central claim was that dealers are OBLIGED to liquidate billions of dollars of stock into the close on expiration Friday, and that claim is false. It appeared in six places, it was the stated cause of both case-study losses, it was the correct answer to both case-study quizzes, it drove the 'never buy calls after 3 PM' rule, and it was the premise of the entire nine-part trading playbook. Correcting it meant rewriting the spine.

fixed: 'A 2020 SEC study found... $1.5 billion/year.' No such study. Removed and replaced with what the evidence actually shows: academic work sending identical orders through multiple brokers simultaneously found large, persistent differences in the prices that came back, while brokers' own Rule 605 execution-quality reports show most marketable retail orders receiving some price improvement. Both are true, and the real argument is about the size of the improvement rather than about being filled outside the quote.

Spoofing, layering and quote stuffing were attributed to market makers as routine practice — 'MM posts fake sell order', 'market maker manipulation', 'illegal-but-common'. The enforcement record is overwhelmingly against proprietary traders, individuals and bank desks, not the registered wholesalers that fill retail orders. Reattributed throughout, with what the prosecutions have actually been.

The spoofing detection rule: 'orders 5-10x larger than surrounding levels that vanish within 60 seconds = 80% likely spoofing; track ten and if eight vanish you have confirmed it.' This is wrong in a way that matters. The great majority of orders in US equities are cancelled rather than executed and have been for over a decade — eight of ten vanishing is what you see in a market with no spoofing in it at all. Replaced with the usable version: do not lean on a large resting order, whatever the intent behind it.

The PFOF quiz scenario, which does not hold together: it posits a seller resting at $100.01 on NYSE while the fill happens at $100.02. If that were so, $100.01 would BE the national best offer and the fill would be a trade-through — a violation, not a loophole. Rewritten around the real complaint, which is that no one else got to compete for the right to fill the order.

'Citadel receives your order 2 milliseconds before public exchanges... Why it's legal.' Trading ahead of a customer order is prohibited. The same class of error as the Citadel claim corrected in lesson 36.

'Market sell orders are ALWAYS filled at the bid.' Marketable retail orders frequently receive price improvement between the quotes — it is the main thing wholesalers sell to brokers — and an order larger than the displayed size walks the book and does worse.

The PFOF rate of $0.002/share for equities, roughly ten times too high, and every dollar figure built on it (Robinhood's $36M, Citadel's $180M, the $144M net). Removed rather than recalculated: the per-share rate is not published in a form you can multiply, and the argument does not need a total.

Two internal contradictions: 'trade illiquid times, pre-market has less HFT activity' directly against Strategy #2's 'avoid after-hours, spreads are 15x wider'; and AAPL's opening spread quoted as 5x wider in one place and 8x in another, same stock, same morning.

The IEX speed bump described as preventing front-running of retail orders — it protects orders RESTING on IEX from stale-quote pickoff, and does nothing for a marketable order sent there. The blanket 'Fidelity, Vanguard, Interactive Brokers don't take PFOF' list, wrong in the details about all three. The $300 million attributed to microwave towers, which actually belongs to the fibre line the microwaves made obsolete. Sarao presented as the cause of the Flash Crash, which the official joint report attributed to a large sell algorithm.

Eric's prior-year winning record (+$87K on 2,400 trades) and his recovery record ($72K to $110K, 52% to 67%), repeated four times. The $68,000 loss stays, and so does the arithmetic that produced it. The cost model was also corrected: most of the $0.10 a share was the spread, which a market order pays by definition and which was wide because of WHEN he traded — a dime a share is not reachable in SPY at 11 AM, and saying so makes the lesson narrower and more useful.
40-market-maker-algorithms.kept: Spread capture and why the spread exists, the adverse-selection section and the three detection signals, inventory management, the latency and co-location material, the whole of Part 6, and all three knowledge-check answers, whose letters are unchanged.
40-market-maker-algorithms.notes: Graded C rather than B because of the evidence problems specifically: a fabricated regulator citation and repeated unsupported allegations of criminal conduct against named firms are a different class of defect from an over-flattering number, and this lesson had both. The teaching survives the corrections almost intact, which is the frustrating part — the case for using limit orders never needed a villain, and the conspiratorial framing was doing no work that the arithmetic was not already doing better.
40-market-maker-algorithms.summary: The advice in this lesson is right and most retail traders need it: your execution costs are real, they compound with frequency, and the fix is limit orders, liquid hours, and knowing how your broker routes. Eric's case study makes the arithmetic concrete in a way that is hard to argue with — $0.10 a share, 300 shares, 60 trades a day, and the edge is gone before you have been wrong about anything. The spread-capture and adverse-selection sections are clear and correct. What earns the C is the evidence: a citation to a regulator study that does not exist, repeated accusations of criminal conduct against named firms, a quiz scenario that contradicts its own premise, and a spoofing-detection rule that would have a reader seeing manipulation in the ordinary behaviour of every order book in the country.

fixed: The central claim — 'QE = liquidity expanding = bullish, QT = liquidity contracting = bearish' — is refuted by 2023 and 2024, in both of which the Fed ran quantitative tightening all year and the S&P gained roughly 24% and then 23%. The lesson asserted the rule in six places and never mentioned the two years that break it. Corrected throughout, and the correction strengthens the lesson rather than weakening it: the RRP drained roughly $2T over the same period, offsetting the balance-sheet runoff, which is precisely why Part 2's three-term net-liquidity measure exists. The balance sheet is now presented as one term of three rather than as the answer.

The Quick Wins list told the reader to check WALCL every Sunday and read a falling line as bearish — the exact instruction the 2023-24 record refutes. Rewritten to send the reader to Part 2 before acting on a falling balance sheet.

A run of invented hit rates and percentages attached to macro claims, none of which anyone has measured over a sample that exists: two QE cycles and two QT cycles is four observations, and the lesson was quoting rates off them.

The two-hour rule's positive form — 'holds into the close, buy tomorrow; fades into the close, short tomorrow' — is a coin flip dressed as a rule, with no evidence offered anywhere in the lesson. Kept the negative form, which is genuinely useful: stay out of the window where spreads are widest and the first move is most often wrong. The 'spreads widen 3-5x' multiple was replaced with the instruction to measure it once on your own instrument.

Absolutist position-sizing prescriptions — specific percentage portfolios per regime, presented as what to hold rather than as illustrations — plus 'every pullback is a gift', which is the sentence that gets a reader fully invested into the pullback that is not.
41-fed-policy-liquidity.kept: The whole of Part 2. The mechanics of TGA and RRP, why a Treasury refill drains reserves and why RRP drawdown adds them, are correctly described and are the part of this subject most retail commentary gets wrong. The FOMC-day discipline (size down or sit out, no market orders in the first minutes, the announcement is not a trade) is sound and stays. The Fed Put section's existing caveats.
41-fed-policy-liquidity.notes: Evidence graded C because the headline thesis was contradicted by the most recent two years and the lesson quoted rates off a four-observation sample. Delivers graded B rather than lower because the machinery the lesson promises — a way to read macro liquidity that is better than watching the balance sheet — is actually delivered in Part 2; the thesis that failed was the simplified version in Part 1, and Part 2 already contained its own correction.
41-fed-policy-liquidity.summary: The best-organised lesson in this stretch, and the net-liquidity construction at its centre is genuinely worth the reader's time: Fed balance sheet minus the Treasury General Account minus the reverse repo facility, each term explained by what it physically does to reserves in the banking system, with the FRED series named so the reader can plot it themselves. The Fed Put section was already nuanced before I touched it — it correctly said the strike moves, that it is not a promise, and that 2022 is the counter-example. Where the lesson failed was its headline thesis, which the two most recent years flatly contradict.

fixed: The SKEW index moves the opposite way from the direction this lesson assumed. Because it measures the out-of-the-money tail relative to at-the-money, SKEW typically FALLS in a panic — at-the-money implied volatility rises faster than the tail — and it runs high in calm markets. It fell during the COVID crash; its record above 170 came in June 2021 with the S&P at an all-time high and VIX in the mid-teens. The lesson had 'SKEW >155 = extreme fear, crash fears overdone → sell OTM puts', a worked example claiming SKEW 'spiked to 157' during the March 2023 banking crisis (it went down), and a quiz answer built on the same premise. Corrected in five places. The March 2023 trade survives on its own merits, because it never actually depended on the index reading — only on the ten-point gap between two implied volatilities you can see on any option chain.

The flagship long-volatility example claimed VIX April $20 calls went from $0.85 to $18.50 during Volmageddon — a 21-bagger — because spot VIX more than doubled. VIX options settle against the VIX FUTURE for their expiration month, not against spot. The April future went from the middle teens to the low twenties; that call was worth a few dollars. The enormous multiples that week were in February and March. This is arguably the most important single fact in VIX trading and the lesson had it exactly backwards in its own worked example, so the correction is now stated as a mechanical fact in Part 1 and demonstrated where the error was.

The 'VIX Mean Reversion Statistics (2000-2024)' table quoted a frequency for each band and a 'percent lower 30 days later' figure running from 92% to 18%. Those were not measured, and the methodology they imply is the error the case study is about: VIX above 40 is not thousands of independent trials since 2000, it is four or five episodes each contributing dozens of overlapping daily observations that all resolve together. Columns removed, direction kept, reasoning stated.

The October 2023 example ran its price path backwards. VIX did not spike from 13.6 to 22 on the October 7 attack; it was already near 17 and closed lower on the 9th while equities rallied, reaching roughly 21.7 on October 20 before falling to about 15 by November 3. Rewritten from the actual sequence — which is a better lesson, because the trade taken on the date the old version recommended spends ten days losing and gets stopped out by the lesson's own stop rule before being proved right.

The case study's contract counts were off by a factor of ten throughout: '15x VIX $15/$18 call spreads, max risk $45K' is $4,500 of risk, not $45,000. Corrected to 150/100/80 spreads, which makes every dollar figure in the story consistent — and reveals the real point: at about $0.35 credit on a $3-wide spread, the position's entire upside was roughly $11,000 against $99,000 of risk. She was risking nine dollars to make one, visible on the screen before the first trade. The reported mark of '+$16,800 (98% max profit)' was impossible, since max profit on a short spread is the credit collected; corrected to about $8,600.

'Kelly Criterion' was used to label what is actually an expectancy calculation. Both are now named correctly, and the conclusion sharpened: a negative expectancy makes the Kelly size negative, which is not 'size down' — it means the correct position was the other side of the trade or none at all.

SVXY was described as 'the inverse of VXX' with '+5 to +15% per month' and 2017's +185% quoted as its track record. SVXY has been a -0.5x product since February 2018; the instrument that returned 185% no longer trades. UVXY was described as 2x; it has been 1.5x since the same date. Both corrected, along with the symmetric decay claim — a daily-rebalanced inverse does not earn the decay of what it inverts.

'Net debit: $15 (this is your max risk)' on a position that is short an SPX straddle. It is not. Corrected, along with the note that the sketch's legs are mismatched by orders of magnitude because a real dispersion book is vega-weighted.

A Quick Win told the reader that buying SVXY when VIX hit 60-80 in March 2020 'profited massively'. Anyone who did that in the second week of March watched it fall for another week first. The framework table's 'sell VIX calls' also contradicted the lesson's own risk warning against naked VIX calls, in three places.
42-volatility-trading-strategies.kept: The VIX-to-expected-range table, which is correct and genuinely clarifying. The whole risk warning. The contango/backwardation term-structure explanation and the 2017 roll-decay example, which is accurately described. The entire case study, whose moral — an 84% win rate with a nine-to-one loss ratio is a losing strategy — is the most important thing in the lesson and is now supported by arithmetic that survives being checked.
42-volatility-trading-strategies.notes: Graded C for the same reason as lessons 39 and 40: the defects were mechanical rather than promotional, and a reader who trusted them would have bought the wrong VIX expiration, read the SKEW index backwards, and shorted volatility into a falling knife on the lesson's own instruction. The corrections make this a better lesson than the average B in this tier — the VIX-options-settle-against-futures point and the SKEW inversion are both things most retail material gets wrong — but the grade records the state the lesson was found in.
42-volatility-trading-strategies.summary: Ambitious and, in places, the best writing in this tier: the opening table converting a VIX level into an expected daily and monthly range is arithmetically correct and is the single most useful thing on the page, and the case study is the most valuable disaster in the curriculum — a trader who won 84% of her trades and was destroyed anyway, because probability is not magnitude. But four separate factual inversions sit between those two poles, and two of them tell the reader to take a specific dangerous trade. The corrections were substantial enough that the lesson now argues with its own earlier self in several places, which is the honest way to leave it.

fixed: The central correction. 'Stocks vs Bonds (Inverse Correlation -0.3 to -0.7)' was presented as structural. The sign of that correlation depends on which shock dominates: growth shocks give the inverse relationship everyone knows, inflation and rates shocks flip it positive, and 2022 was the clearest positive-correlation year in decades — the S&P and long Treasuries both fell, which is why 60/40 had its worst year in a century. Rewritten as a conditional, which makes the rest of the lesson cohere: the autumn 2023 case study is a rates-shock episode, so TLT falling alongside SPY was the mechanism, not a divergence from it.

The rule that followed from the error: 'SPY + TLT both down >1% same day → exit ALL risk positions, go to cash, wait for correlations to normalize (usually 1-4 weeks).' Applied to 2022 that instruction leaves you in cash for two years waiting for a normalisation that is not coming, because nothing is broken. Replaced with the test that actually distinguishes a liquidation from a rates repricing: in a liquidation the dollar and cash are the only things bid and the selling is indiscriminate; in a repricing the selling is orderly, credit behaves, gold often holds.

'January 2020: SPY at all-time highs, HYG lagging, credit spreads widening. 2 months later: COVID crash. Credit warned first.' It did not. High-yield spreads were near cycle tights in January 2020 and HYG turned within a day of SPY in late February. This mattered because it was the flagship example for the signal the lesson calls most reliable. Replaced with a warning about hindsight-fitting the divergence.

The copper lead time. 'Copper moves 2-4 weeks BEFORE stocks' was contradicted by the lesson's own example: copper peaked on 20 May 2024, SPY not until 16 July — a two-month lead, during which selling on the copper signal would have cost an 8% rally. The example was also mis-dated to July. Corrected in four places, with the honest characterisation: usually early, sometimes very early, occasionally wrong, and therefore a reason to stop adding rather than a reason to go flat.

The composite's after-record: '18 trades, 14 winners, +$21K, $91K → $112K (+23%)' over Nov 2023 - Feb 2024. That window was one of the strongest four-month equity runs in years; almost any long held through it made money, so the figure measures the rally rather than the checklist. Removed, and replaced with what the checklist actually said on the relevant dates, which is checkable.

'When yields rise this fast, stocks MUST fall', twice, plus '+85 bps in 8 weeks — historic move', also twice. 2013 and 2021 are both counter-examples to the first and 2022 produced several larger moves than the second.

'About 40% of S&P 500 revenue comes from overseas' — the figure has been closer to 30% for some years. 'Q1 2022: SPY dropped from $480 to $410 over the same quarter' — that took until mid-May, which matters because it makes the dollar signal early rather than coincident. 'When 10Y yield spikes +10 bps, SPY typically drops 0.5-1.0%' and 'saves 50% of confusion', both invented.
'Real Trade Examples / Live Trades' relabelled as worked reconstructions, with the note that they cannot show you the occasions when the same signals lined up and the market went the other way.
43-cross-market-correlation.kept: Everything that checks out, which is most of it. The March 2020 forced-liquidation table. The dollar transmission mechanism. The credit-divergence logic, now with an honest example. Both Part 4 setups, whose prices and dates I verified line by line. The daily checklist, which is the lesson's real deliverable and is well constructed.
43-cross-market-correlation.notes: Graded B rather than A because the headline relationship was taught with the wrong sign for the very period the case study covers, and because a reader following the high-correlation rule through 2022 would have sat in cash for two years. Graded B rather than C because the underlying market data is unusually accurate, the reasoning is sound wherever the regime question does not arise, and the correction strengthens rather than undermines the lesson: knowing which side of zero the stock/bond correlation is on is more useful than any of the rules it replaced.
43-cross-market-correlation.summary: The best-sourced lesson in this stretch. The March 2020 cross-asset table is accurate to within a point or two on every line, the September 2022 short and the November 2023 long check out against the actual prices and dates, and the November 2023 quiz example (SPY +8.9%, TLT +9.5% in the same month) is exactly right. That is rare enough in this curriculum to be worth stating. The defect is conceptual rather than factual: the lesson teaches the stock/bond correlation as a fixed inverse relationship, and its own case study is drawn from a period when the two fell together for eight straight weeks.

fixed: The case study. A 100-share order in NVDA was said to have been detected in 2 milliseconds, front-run with a 10,000-share purchase, and sold back 82 cents higher. Three things are wrong with that. A 100-share order in a mega-cap carries no information and is a rounding error against the day's volume. No firm takes on several million dollars of inventory to extract eighty-two dollars. And the story's own numbers do not close: the HFT makes several thousand dollars while the victim loses eighty-two, so whoever is paying, it is not him. The date was impossible too — NVDA split ten-for-one in June 2024 and traded near $135 in October, not $875. Rewritten so the loss stays (it is real and it is the point) and the diagnosis changes: he was sending market orders into fast books and walking up the depth, which needs no villain.

The counterfactual saving. 'December: slippage dropped to $0.18, about $5,600 saved in one month.' That is a guess about trades that did not happen, dressed as a measurement. Removed, with the reason stated, since a lesson that spends five parts teaching scepticism about numbers should not end on one.

'Win rate of 95%+ because they only take statistically favorable trades.' This is a misreading of Virtu's IPO disclosure of one losing DAY in 1,238 trading days. Per trade a market maker loses constantly; the business is the aggregate. Corrected, with the source of the confusion named.

Six invented strategy shares that summed neatly to 100% (market making 40%, latency arb 25%, stat arb 20%, order anticipation 10%, event arb 3%, maker-taker 2%). Nobody outside the firms knows the split. Removed, with the ordering kept because the ordering is the useful part.

Two detection heuristics that describe the ordinary market rather than anything unusual. 'Order cancellation rate: normal 20-40%, HFT active 95-99.9% = quote stuffing or spoofing' — almost all orders are cancelled in every name all day; that is the baseline. 'Odd lots of 17, 83, 241 shares = HFT inventory management' — odd lots are about half of all US equity trades now and a large share come from retail brokers and fractional orders. Both were the lesson-40 error repeated: a reader applying them concludes manipulation is everywhere.

The IEX defence misdescribed the speed bump. The coil delays inbound orders while IEX's own market-data view is not delayed, and that asymmetry protects orders RESTING on the book, not orders crossing the spread — so it does nothing for the marketable order the lesson is telling the reader to protect. Added the part every article omits: at a broker that sells order flow, marketable orders never reach an exchange at all.

'HFT firms see your order 50,000x-200,000x faster than you see theirs' — a category error. Speed determines who reacts first to public information; it gives nobody a private view of your intentions. The wholesaler that sees your order sees it because it is the counterparty.

The institution's $175,000 of slippage on 500,000 TSLA shares was attributed wholly to being anticipated. Most of it is the fund's own market impact, which exists in a market with no HFT in it. 'Firms earn back $100M in 6-18 months', 'market orders cost ~$70/trade in HFT tax', 'IEX saves $500-1,500 over 100 trades' — all invented. 'Patience is free money' — it is not: waiting out a spread during a 2% decline swaps a certain cost for an uncertain one.

The 5 August 2024 open was attributed to quote stuffing. It was a liquidity vacuum from an overnight carry unwind. Also corrected the direction-blind claim that waiting 'saved 1-2%' — true if you were selling, expensive if you were buying.
44-hft-mechanics.kept: Everything about latency and infrastructure. The Flash Crash timeline. The enforcement history. The maker-taker arithmetic, which is correct. All five defences, which are sound execution hygiene even though the lesson arrived at them by way of a threat model that needed correcting. The reframed opening now says the honest thing: for a retail trader in a liquid name HFT is mostly a subsidy, and the situations where it is a tax are all things the reader controls.
44-hft-mechanics.notes: Graded C for the same class of reason as 39, 40 and 42: the errors are mechanical and several of them are instructions. A reader who believed the case study would conclude that their 100-share orders are being hunted, would go looking for a routing fix that does not address their problem, and would use two detection heuristics that flag the entire market. The corrections leave the lesson shorter on drama and much more useful.
44-hft-mechanics.summary: The infrastructure half of this lesson is genuinely good — colocation, microwave routes, FPGAs, why a Chicago-to-New Jersey round trip on fibre and on microwave differ by several milliseconds. The Flash Crash account is accurate down to the 75,000 E-mini contracts and the 2:47 pm low, and the enforcement citations (Citadel Securities $22.6M in 2017, Tower Research $67M in 2019, JPMorgan $920M in 2020) are correct and correctly attributed. What sits between those is a lesson organised around a threat that does not exist in the form described, and a case study whose central mechanism is arithmetically impossible.

fixed: The missing idea, now stated: the imbalance is PUBLISHED. It goes to everyone on the same feed at the same instant, so a good part of the move it implies has already happened by the time you have read the number and clicked. The lesson treated it as though it were private information the reader was lucky to find. It is a regulatory disclosure, and markets absorb disclosures quickly. What remains tradeable is the residual, which is smaller than the headline size suggests. This reframes the whole strategy section honestly: a large imbalance is worth a great deal as a reason not to be positioned against it, and rather less as a reason to be positioned with it.

Five invented hit rates: '65-70% directional' above 5M shares, '70-75%' above 10M, 'the win rate on these setups is 70-75%' in the sizing section, 'roughly 70-75% of the time' in the Quick Wins, and 'about 80% of the time' in a quiz answer. None measured. The lesson's own Part 3 already said 'we are not going to put win rates on either' — so it refused to quote a figure in one section while quoting one in five others. All removed.

The expected-move ladder attached to each imbalance band (0.05-0.15%, 0.15-0.30%, 0.30-0.60%+) was invented. Replaced with what is actually true: the relationship is real in direction and the magnitude depends on the day's resting liquidity, on whether the imbalance gets offset before the print, and on what else is happening in the last ten minutes.

The index-inclusion effect. 'Stocks rally 5-15% from announcement to effective date' comes from research on the 1990s and 2000s. It has shrunk close to zero in recent years, for the obvious reason: everyone knows about it, so it prices on the announcement. Corrected — which makes Strategy 1 much less attractive, honestly so. The Tesla numbers stay because they are correct, and the existing note that Tesla was an outlier at 1.7% index weight is exactly right.
The MOO publication times were Nasdaq's presented as both exchanges'. NYSE begins disseminating opening imbalance information from 8:00 AM, not 9:28.

The MOO quiz answer claimed the order type gives 'no slippage'. An MOO is a market order into the auction and fills at whatever the clearing price is, which on a gap morning can be far from the prior close. What it avoids is walking the book. Corrected, and the invented '$0.05-0.15/share more' removed.

'Do this 4 times before risking real money. If 3/4 worked (75% hit rate), edge validated.' A coin gives three out of four about a third of the time. Raised to twenty, with a clear statement of what twenty does and does not establish. The Quick Wins' 'saves 0.1-0.3% of notional' was also inconsistent with its own worked example, which comes to under a tenth of a percent.

'21 of the 23 trades lost, every one of them held against a 5M-11M share imbalance' — 21 consecutive occasions of a 5M+ imbalance running against him is not a thing that happens. Softened to what he could actually have reconstructed.
45-auction-theory-imbalances.kept: All the mechanics. The Tesla example, verified date by date. The whole spoofing section, which correctly explains why an imbalance that shrinks between updates is usually offsetting interest rather than manipulation. The entry-timing window. The case study, whose ES point-and-dollar arithmetic is right throughout and whose lesson — check the feed before you hold into a close — is sound and free.
45-auction-theory-imbalances.notes: Graded B, not C: nothing here was factually broken in the way lessons 39, 40, 42 and 44 were, and the market data that is quoted checks out. The gap was between what the lesson knew in one section and what it claimed in another, plus the missing observation that public information behaves like public information. Fixing the second turns a set of trade recipes into a piece of reasoning the reader can extend.
45-auction-theory-imbalances.summary: Auction mechanics done properly: how the clearing price is chosen, what MOC and LOC orders are, where to find the imbalance feed for free, and why the closing cross is the largest single liquidity event of the day. The Tesla index-addition example is accurate to the dollar on every date I checked, and the ES arithmetic in the case study is correct on every line. A previous pass had already removed the composite's after-record and had already got the spoofing section right, including the point that NYSE MOC orders cannot be cancelled after the 3:50 cutoff. What remained was a set of invented hit rates that the lesson elsewhere explicitly refuses to quote, and one missing idea that changes how the whole thing should be read.

fixed: A wrong option letter in the quiz-3 explanation: the text said 2.24% is 'answer B' when B is 4.58% and C is 2.24%. In a lesson whose whole point is arithmetic, a reader who checks would lose confidence in the rest of it.

The composite's after-record ('$151.6K → $178K, +17.4% in 5 months'), which appeared twice. August to December 2024 was a strong market; five months of long exposure measures the market. Replaced with the part that is a property of the rules rather than the outcome: effective risk capped at 1.2%, never more than three correlated positions.

Task 4 of the practice exercise computed each position's loss as the correlated percentage of the move, while ignoring that four of the five stops sit only 1.1-1.9% away. A 2.5-2.9% adverse move does not cost you the correlated percentage on those — it costs the full stop on each, plus slippage. That is a second lesson hiding in the exercise and it is now stated: tight stops do not make a correlated book safer, they make every position hit its maximum on the same morning.

Rachel's example is arithmetically exact ($160,000 of stock at a 4.1% average fill is $6,560) but never mentions that six positions of $26,700 against an $80,000 account is two times gross exposure. She was thinking in risk percentages instead of position sizes, which is precisely how the 4.1% fill becomes an 8.2% account loss. Now stated.

The tail-hedging section repeated lesson 42's error by omission: it recommended long VIX calls without mentioning that VIX options settle against the VIX future for their expiration month, not spot. Spot going 20 to 80 does not take a four-month future with it, and that is the most common way this hedge disappoints. Also added what 0.5-1% per month actually is (6-12% a year of permanent drag) and what a put spread does to a tail hedge (caps the payoff exactly where the crash gets serious).

CVAR appeared in the Key Takeaways but was never defined. Added, with the reason it matters: a portfolio can have a comfortable VAR and a terrifying CVAR, and that shape is exactly what a short-volatility or heavily correlated book looks like.

'Professionals survive 20 losing trades in a row. Retail blows up after 3.' Replaced with the arithmetic, which makes the same point and is true: twenty losses at half a percent costs a tenth of the account; the same streak at five percent, or at half a percent across six positions that are really one, ends it.
46-advanced-risk-management.kept: The formula and every application of it. The derivation in the quiz-3 answer, which correctly goes from portfolio variance to the working form. The Callum and Rachel case studies, whose dollar arithmetic is right throughout. The heat-limit table with its existing caveat that the 10-15% figures belong to institutional desks. Emma's exercise, including the correlation-matrix averaging over all ten unique pairs. The position-sizing quiz, whose every figure checks out.
46-advanced-risk-management.notes: The first A in this stretch and an earned one. What distinguishes it is that the lesson does not ask you to believe anything: it hands you a formula, shows you where it comes from, and then works it on real numbers you can check. The case studies exist to illustrate a calculation rather than to sell a system, and both of them are internally consistent to the dollar. The defects I found were a wrong letter, an unremoved after-record, and three places where a true statement could be made more precise — which is a different category of problem from the ones in the four lessons before it.
46-advanced-risk-management.summary: The best lesson audited in this stretch, and it is not close. It takes one idea — that adding correlated positions buys you almost no diversification — derives the formula for it correctly from portfolio variance, and then applies that formula in about a dozen places without getting it wrong once. Every number I checked came out right: the 0.92 factor at six positions and 0.82 correlation, the 1.18 effective bets, the 0.41 independent-case factor, the 7.5% on the eight-position example, the convergence to √ρ as N grows. An earlier pass had already added the framing that makes it click — nominal risk is the ceiling you hit when every stop fills at once, and correlation decides how close to that ceiling an ordinary bad day sits. The remaining defects were small and specific.

47-portfolio-construction-kelly.added: The argument the lesson was missing, and the one that does the most work. Kelly assumes p and b are known; they are estimated from a finite sample, and the plug-in fraction is biased upward as a result. On the lesson's own 60%/1.67 example, a hundred trades showing 60% winners puts the true rate somewhere near 50-70%, and the formula returns 36% at the top of that range and 20% at the bottom — a two-to-one swing in position size on a difference a hundred trades cannot resolve. Since overbetting Kelly destroys growth faster than underbetting costs, the error is asymmetric in its consequences. That is a second and independent reason for fractional Kelly, and it is stronger than the variance argument the lesson already had.
fixed: The heat cap said three different things in one lesson. Part 3 correctly sets the retail limit at 6% and explicitly names 10-15% as an institutional-desk figure. The Pro Tip dashboard immediately below it then shows 10.2% heat with a green tick and instructs the reader to wait only above 15%; the practice exercise says a 14.75% book sits 'inside a 15% cap'; and the closing checklist asks whether heat is under 'your 10-15% cap'. Worse, the dashboard produced its 10.2% by putting each strategy's Kelly fraction in the heat column — the exact conflation the paragraph above it warns against. Rebuilt the dashboard so the middle column is risk per open trade and the total is 4.3%, moved every cap reference to 6%, and named the allocation-versus-heat confusion in the text.

Lisa's recovery after-record — 'Switched to 1/4 Kelly (4.2%). Results: $71K to $111K (+56%) in 6 months, max DD -12%' — carried in both the case study and its quiz answer. Removed from both. What replaces it is the part that was always the real evidence: run the identical six-loss streak at 4.2% and 0.958^6 = 0.773 takes $192.5K to $149K instead of $64K. That $85K is arithmetic on a streak that happened. The +56% was a forecast about trades that did not.

The prop-trader worked example did not add up. Old sizing at 2% gave +$140K/year (+28%); new sizing at 3% was reported as +$224K/year (+45%), with the text saying return and drawdown both scaled by roughly 1.5x. The drawdown did (15% to 22%), but 140 x 1.5 is 210, not 224. Corrected to +$210K (+42%), which is what the lesson's own stated scaling requires.

The Three Pillars table put 'Kelly Criterion adjusted for edge strength (5-15% for proven edges)' in the Institutional column. No institution risks 5-15% of the fund on a position; the figure is a retail quarter-Kelly number wearing an institutional label. Replaced with what institutions actually do differently, which is recompute the fraction as the estimate of the edge moves.

Ed Thorp's 'roughly 20% a year for two decades', quoted twice. Princeton/Newport ran 1969-1988 at about 15% net to investors and around 19% gross. The 20% is the gross figure presented without the label. Corrected in both places, with the distinction stated, because a lesson about compounding should not quote the number an investor did not compound at.

The practice exercise closed with 'If the edges hold, expect roughly 15-25% CAGR with 12-18% peak-to-trough drawdowns' — a forward projection invented from three estimated edges. Removed, and replaced with the collision the exercise had accidentally built: quarter Kelly on three real edges asks for 14.75% of the account and the retail heat cap says 6%, so scale all three by 0.41 and size to the smaller constraint.

Equity-curve position sizing was presented as pure upside. Added what it is — a trend-following overlay on your own equity curve — and what it costs: it pays when results cluster and bleeds when they merely alternate, because then you are small into every recovery and large into every drawdown.
47-portfolio-construction-kelly.kept: Every derivation and every worked figure: the two equivalent formulas, the drawdown-and-recovery table, the (2f - f^2) growth fraction, the three-strategy weighting comparison with its 4.5x edge ratio and +28% improvement, Lisa's expectancy and streak arithmetic, the 10-loss equity-curve comparison in Q5, and all three Quick Win stress-test figures (0.80^7, 0.98^7, 0.95^7 all check).
47-portfolio-construction-kelly.notes: Graded B, not A, on one distinction from lesson 46. Both lessons do their mathematics properly, but 46 was consistent with itself and this one was not: a reader who followed Part 3 and a reader who followed the dashboard two inches below it would have run books with two and a half times the risk difference between them. Contradictions inside a single lesson are worse than a merely optimistic claim, because the reader has no way to tell which half to believe.
47-portfolio-construction-kelly.summary: The Kelly mathematics here is genuinely derived and then correctly applied about twenty times, which puts this lesson in the top handful of the curriculum on evidence quality. Both forms of the formula agree, the 60%/1.67 example resolves to 35.9%, the full drawdown table checks out to the decimal (0.641^5 = 0.108 gives -89.2% needing +824% to recover; 0.98^5 gives -9.6% needing +11%), the growth fraction (2f - f^2) is right and its half- and quarter-Kelly values of 75% and 44% are right, the equal-weight versus edge-weight comparison across three strategies is right at every step, and Lisa's case study is arithmetically consistent from expectancy through the six-loss streak. What holds it to a B is that the lesson contradicts itself on the single number a reader is most likely to act on, and that it stops one argument short of the one that matters most.

fixed: The central rule was arithmetically impossible. 'When you see 50M shares bought in 10 minutes, institutions are ACCUMULATING' appeared six times — in the case study result line, the missed-signals list, the breaking-point quote, the recovery rule, the quiz option and the quiz answer. SPY trades roughly 70-90 million shares across all venues in an entire ordinary day. Fifty million in ten minutes is most of a session. The recovery rule also asked for 'sweeps >10M shares', which is not what a sweep is. Rewritten throughout with the real scale stated: a large SPY block is a few hundred thousand shares, a large single-name block is tens of thousands, and if a number quoted at you would be most of the day's volume, the number is wrong.

'Magnet behavior: price gravitates toward VWAP throughout the day (institutions pull it back)' — a causal claim about an arithmetic property. VWAP is the volume-weighted average of every price so far today, so on a directionless day price is mechanically near its own average most of the time. On a trend day price sits on one side of VWAP from open to close and never returns, and no amount of algo activity drags it across. Corrected, along with the practice exercise's 'on 3 or more days out of 5, price will typically revert at least three or four times' and the Quick Win's 'you will find SPY returning to VWAP three to five times' — both invented counts, and both false on precisely the days that matter.

The block-print table inferred intent from a print. Every block has two sides: a 200,000-share print is one institution buying and another selling at a price both accepted, and the print does not say which was the eager one. Added the honest reading before the table — a buy printed above the day's average price means the buyer took worse-than-average execution to get filled, which is weak evidence of urgency, not evidence of conviction or of being right.

'Standalone icebergs can be spoofs' contradicted the lesson's own quiz answer twenty screens later ('icebergs refresh instantly; spoofs get pulled before filling'). A spoof is cancelled before it fills; an iceberg is defined by continuing to fill. Replaced with the alternative explanation that actually competes: a market maker absorbing retail sell orders and hedging elsewhere produces an identical tape and has no directional opinion at all.

DIX described as a 'smart money sentiment' gauge, which contradicts Lesson 36's correction that most off-exchange share volume is wholesaler internalisation of retail orders rather than institutions crossing in dark pools. Reframed as what it is: buying pressure in a stream that is heavily retail, with some documented relationship to forward returns but not the mechanism usually claimed for it.

Ryan's composite after-record ('$99K to $162K, +64% in 7 months, 69% win rate'), carried in the case study and repeated in Quick Win 3 with the flourish 'those two numbers — 28% fading it, 69% joining it — are the whole argument'. Removed from both; the disaster record and the 19-of-67 count stay, because those are counts of trades that happened.

'DIX divergences are high-probability reversal signals' in an exercise whose entire purpose is to have the reader measure that frequency for themselves, and a 'win rate boost' claim on a worked trade.
48-institutional-order-flow.kept: The TWAP and VWAP signature sections with their worked tapes, the five-step iceberg detection walkthrough and its absorption-ratio arithmetic, the block-size and iceberg-signal tables, the institutional timing windows, and all three worked trades — whose figures check out ($1.15 x 300 = $345, $1.80 x 200 = $360, $4.90 x 150 = $735).
48-institutional-order-flow.notes: Close to a C. What holds it at B is that the two best sections — how a VWAP algo behaves around fair value and how to read an iceberg off the tape — are correct, concrete and hard to find explained this well elsewhere. But the pattern here is worth naming, because it recurs: the lesson knew the mechanism and then attached a number to it that nobody checked. The mechanism was the valuable part all along.
48-institutional-order-flow.summary: The mechanics are the strong half and they are mostly right. The TWAP and VWAP execution signatures are described the way those algorithms actually behave, the iceberg walkthrough is the best step-by-step in this stretch of the curriculum — identify the level, watch the absorption, compute the ratio, wait for the bid to be pulled — and the institutional timing table is sensible. What drags the grade down is that the lesson's headline rule was built on a quantity that does not exist, and that two of its explanations get the mechanism backwards. A reader who took the mechanics and ignored the rules would have done well; a reader who took the rules would have been waiting for a signal that cannot occur.
48-institutional-order-flow.tooling: numcheck could not license a spelled-out range shared across its unit. It already knew that '$3-5K' means 3,000 to 5,000, but '70-90 million' licensed only 90,000,000, so the Japanese rendering of the lower bound as a myriad (7,000万) failed. Taught it that a spelled-out range shares its word the same way a suffixed one does.

fixed: The regime score adds volatility and trend as if they were one axis. ADX above 25 scores +1 for trending, ATR above 1.5x scores +1 for volatile, BB Width above 8% scores +1 for expanded — so a chaotic news-driven session scores +3 before the VWAP and volume terms are counted, reading 'strong trending, trade pullbacks and breakouts' on exactly the day the lesson elsewhere says to sit out. The practice exercise then bolts on a 'High Volatility override' to undo it, which is an admission the single number does not work. Split into a trend score and a volatility reading kept beside it, with both required before sizing up.

Both composites carried complete after-records. Sarah: '6 trades, 83% WR, recovered $4,200 ... recovered $11,800 ... 3-month summary: recovered $16,000, account $51,700 ... 17 trades, 0 in the wrong regime, regime match 100%.' Marcus: 'Feb +$2.2K, Mar 73% WR +$14.6K, Apr 78% WR +$11.8K, 3-month recovery +$28,640 (+27.6%), final $132K.' Both removed. Both replaced with the countable change, which was always the real evidence: Sarah went from 38 trades in eight weeks to 17 in twelve; Marcus took 4 trades in a range month where the comparable stretch before had produced 15.

The headline statistic was four trades. 'She had a 75% win rate when ADX > 25 (4 trades: 3W/1L)' was repeated as '75% win rate in trends' in the closing summary, the Key Takeaways, the Quick Wins and the quiz answer. Three out of four is not a win rate. Rewritten to put the weight where it belongs: 7 winners in 34 trades losing $41,700 is a result luck does not produce, and it establishes the negative claim, which is the useful one.

Both stories were dated onto quarters that contradict them. Sarah's reflection claims the market trended 80% of the time in Q4 2023 and only 10% of the time in Q1 2024 — but Q1 2024 was one of the strongest and steadiest first quarters on record for US equities, not a chop. Marcus's disaster is dated Nov 2023 to Jan 2024 with 'SPY chopping $440-460 for 11 weeks', which is the sharpest two-month rally in years described as a range. Dates removed from both, with the reason stated in the text: date a composite and someone will pull up the chart.

The deeper statistical problem, which neither case study acknowledged and which is now stated in three places: regimes arrive in blocks of weeks, so 'my trending trades' and 'my ranging trades' are two consecutive stretches of one account. Any strategy compared across a good period and a bad period shows this gap whether or not the regime caused it. Marcus's 18-of-24 against 12-of-45 is a real gap and worth acting on; it is not a controlled test of ADX, and the lesson now says so.

The practice exercise told the reader its own answer before they measured. 'You'll likely find 60-80% win rate when matches, 20-40% when doesn't' — removed. 'Target accuracy: 7+ out of 10 correct classifications = system working' — replaced with the base-rate point: if seven of ten days were ranging, always answering 'ranging' scores 7 out of 10 without looking at an indicator.

'This one filter can double your profitability', 'trending regimes have 2-3x higher expectancy than ranging', 'DIX divergences are high-probability reversal signals', 'if you don't check ADX before EVERY trade, you're gambling', 'you're in the top 5% of traders', and the compression card's 'THE most predictable regime shift' — which contradicted the lesson's own Bollinger section saying a squeeze tells you neither when nor which way.
49-market-regime-recognition.kept: The four-regime taxonomy and its per-regime strategy and avoid lists, the ADX band table, the ATR-ratio classification, the Bollinger Width thresholds, the regime-adaptive sizing ladder, the institutional timing windows, and both disaster records — Sarah's 38 trades for -$39,300 with the rule-by-rule savings breakdown (which is internally consistent: 21,400 + 16,400 + 3,900 = 41,700 across 18 + 12 + 4 = 34 trades), and Marcus's -$43,280 month by month.
49-market-regime-recognition.notes: Graded C. The gap between the quality of the idea and the quality of the evidence offered for it is the widest in the curriculum so far. Every single number the lesson used to prove its thesis was either invented, computed on four trades, dated onto a market that did the opposite, or confounded by comparing consecutive time periods. The idea survives all of that intact, which is itself the point worth making to the reader: you do not need a fabricated win rate to justify checking whether your strategy's conditions are present. Counting how many trades you took outside them is enough, and unlike a win rate, it is knowable tonight.
49-market-regime-recognition.summary: The idea at the centre of this lesson is genuinely one of the most useful in the curriculum: a strategy has conditions, those conditions come and go, and most traders never check whether today's conditions are the ones their edge was built for. The four-regime taxonomy is clean, the ADX/ATR/Bollinger toolkit is the right toolkit, and the framing that regime detection comes first and strategy selection second is correct. Then the lesson tries to prove it, and the proof is where everything goes wrong. Two composite case studies, both with full invented recovery records, both dated onto calendar periods that did the opposite of what the story requires, and a headline statistic that rests on four trades. The scoring system it hands you is also internally broken in a way the lesson half-notices and patches over.

50-auction-theory-advanced.added: The two opening patterns the lesson promised in its own What You'll Master list, listed again in the Key Takeaways, tested in the quiz, and never actually described: Open-Drive and Open-Test-Drive. Both now get what each commits you to and what invalidates it — including the point that Open-Drive is the one pattern arguing for a trend day, and therefore against every mean-reversion idea in Part 3.
fixed: The central mechanical error, and the most valuable correction in this lesson: a fair value gap is not a gap. The three-candle shape means candle 1's high sits below candle 3's low — but every price in that range printed, during candle 2, and somebody was filled at each of them. What the pattern marks is displacement: a move fast enough that the bars either side do not overlap. That is real and worth watching. It is not untraded price, and no auction principle requires a return to it. The lesson's auction analogy ('the auctioneer skipped $520, so someone yells about it') was doing the wrong work entirely, and the genuinely untraded gaps — overnight and across halts — got named for the first time.

The FVG fill statistics table (70-80% same session, 85-90% within 24 hours, 95%+ within three days), quoted again in the Aha Moment and again in the Key Takeaways. No such figure exists on an inspectable sample, and the base rate destroys it anyway: an intraday FVG is a zone a few cents wide near the current price, and price revisits almost any such zone within a day. Worse, the gaps that matter most — the wide ones left by a trend day — are precisely the ones that do not fill. Replaced with a counting exercise that records gap width, time to touch, whether it held the midpoint, and the day type, because that last column is where the answer actually lives.

Emma's case study contradicted its own moral. Her review split $71,000 into $7,014 of execution cost and $64,000 of directional loss — and the lesson then declared 'auction illiteracy' the fatal mistake, with a quiz question marking that answer correct. Nine dollars in ten came from being wrong about direction. Question and options rewritten so the correct answer is the split itself: separate what your ideas cost from what your fills cost, then work on whichever is bigger.

The slippage figures were off by a factor of thirty to sixty. '$0.30-0.60/share midday' in SPY and QQQ, stated five times. Both quote a one-cent spread for essentially the whole session and a retail order rests inside it. Half-dollar slippage on 200 shares of SPY comes from market orders or from a far less liquid instrument, not from the hour. Corrected with the diagnosis that actually applies, plus a Quick Win that has the reader measure their own.

'Exit at 3:58 PM MOC', instructed four times. The MOC cut-off is 3:50 PM on both NYSE and Nasdaq; after that new MOC orders are rejected. The instruction cannot be followed. Corrected, keeping what is true — the closing auction is routinely the largest single print of the day.

'Enter ONLY at 9:31-9:35 AM' — the open has the highest volume and also the widest spreads, the most volatility and the most adverse selection, and the rule contradicts the lesson's own Part 1, since you cannot read an opening range that does not exist yet. Removed, and the execution advice reduced to the part that actually does the work at retail size: use limits, not market orders.
