'Above POC = expensive, below POC = cheap', stated in the section heading, the Key Takeaways and the practice exercise. The POC is where the most volume traded in a window you chose. In an uptrend price is above yesterday's POC every day and keeps going, and a trader reading that as expensive shorts the whole trend. Reframed as a map of where two-sided trade should be expected, with the day type from Part 1 deciding whether it is tradable.

'Performance is typically 65-70%+ at the exact VAH/VAL touch', 'trade FVG fills with 70%+ accuracy', 'Success criteria: 7+ out of 10' (replaced with the base-rate point), 'your expectancy skyrockets', 'floor trader-level mastery', 'you're in the top 5% of traders', and the invented winning outcome attached to the five-way confluence setup.
50-auction-theory-advanced.kept: The Open-Rejection-Reverse and Open-Balance descriptions, the three-candle FVG definition and both worked trades (whose R:R arithmetic checks: $0.60 risk against $2.40 and $2.20 of reward gives 4.0R and 3.7R), the value area structure, the Plutus and Janus integration examples, and the five-part practice exercise, which is well designed once its pre-announced answers are removed.
50-auction-theory-advanced.notes: Graded C. The distinguishing feature here is not exaggeration but explanation: three separate times, the lesson attached a plausible-sounding mechanism to a real observation, and each mechanism was wrong in a way that changes what the reader does. A trader who believes an FVG is untraded price will wait for fills that were never owed; one who believes the POC is a valuation will fade a trend all the way up; one who believes midday costs half a dollar a share will restructure their day around a cost that is one cent. The observations underneath all three survive, which is why the lesson is worth repairing rather than cutting.
50-auction-theory-advanced.summary: Three good subjects, and the lesson gets the mechanism wrong on all three. Opening patterns are the right first read on a session, fair value gaps mark something real, and the value area is a genuine map of where an auction has done its business. But the lesson taught FVGs as untraded price when the zone demonstrably traded, taught the POC as a valuation when it is a backward-looking mode, and built a whole case study on a slippage figure roughly thirty to sixty times too large for the instruments named. It also promised four opening patterns, described two, and then set a quiz question on one of the two it never taught.

51-cross-asset-correlations.added: A Part 1, which the lesson had been missing — it opened at Part 2 — covering what a correlation can and cannot do for you, and giving the reader the distinction the rest of the lesson depends on. Plus the mechanism behind the SPY-and-VIX-rising 'divergence': VIX reflects demand for protection, and demand rises ahead of known events, so a large share of those occurrences are people buying insurance on a calendar date rather than a short-covering rally.
fixed: The lesson's thesis was that cross-assets lead equities by 12-48 hours, TNX leads SPY by 1-3 days, and Nasdaq leads crypto by 6-24 hours. None of that is true, and the reason matters: SPY, TLT, DXY, GLD and VIX trade at the same time in the same market, and a relationship that reliably paid off a day later would be arbitraged away in an afternoon. The VIX case is the clearest — it is calculated from SPX option prices, so asking whether it leads SPY is asking whether the thermometer leads the temperature. Replaced throughout with what these relationships are actually worth, which is context: they tell you what conditions your setup has to survive, available before you click.

One real exception preserved and correctly explained: crypto trades 24 hours and US cash equities do not, so an overnight futures move genuinely does precede the cash open. That is not one market leading another; it is one market being open when the other is shut. The lesson's crypto trade setup now says that instead of promising a 6-24 hour head start.

'SPY vs TNX: typical correlation negative' stated flatly, in a curriculum where Lesson 43 already corrects this. The sign depends on what is driving yields: an inflation or policy story compresses valuations and equities fall, but a growth scare sends yields down and equities down together. The stock-bond correlation was negative in the other direction for most of the two decades before 2022 — that is why 60/40 worked — and it flipped in 2022. Regime question now precedes the relationship.
'TNX +0.5% → SPY drops 3-5% within 1-3 days' — an invented magnitude on an invented lead time. Removed, with the note that 50bp on the 10-year in three days is itself an enormous move.

The correlation coefficients were inflated. DXY/gold quoted at -0.7 to -0.9 and called 'one of the most reliable correlations in macro'; on daily returns over long samples it is closer to -0.3 to -0.5 and has gone positive for months when both were bid as havens. BTC/QQQ quoted at a fixed 0.6-0.8, which describes 2022 and not the long periods where it sat near zero. Both corrected, keeping the mechanisms, which are sound.

Chris's after-record — '26% WR → 72% WR, recovered from $86K to $138K (+60%) in 3 months' — survived in the quiz answer after an earlier pass had removed it from the body. Removed. The 17-of-23 count stays, because it counts trades that happened.
Two dated trades placed on weekend days: 'May 12' (a Sunday) and 'Aug 3' (a Saturday) in 2024. Dates removed rather than shifted, with the reason stated.

'VIX > 30 Panic → Sit out OR buy dips' — two opposite instructions in one table cell. 'Macro beats micro. Every. Single. Time.' 'This one habit prevents 30%+ of losing trades.' 'Performance is typically 65-70%+' on the VIX-divergence fade. 'Divergences typically close within 1-3 days and usually close in DXY's direction.' And the SEO description on all three social tags, which read 'Bonds lead, dollar drives, gold warns. Learn intermarket analysis to see moves before they happen.'
51-cross-asset-correlations.kept: The pre-market checklist, the Confluence Matrix with its bullish and bearish counts and decision rule, the VIX band table, the gold-and-oil interpretation, the six-part practice exercise, and the mechanism behind every correlation discussed — because the mechanisms are right even where the coefficients and lead times were not.
51-cross-asset-correlations.notes: Graded C. This is the third lesson in this stretch (with 48 and 50) where a sound observation was wrapped in an invented mechanism, and it is the most consequential of the three, because a reader who believes bonds warn them a day early will wait for a signal that never arrives and will mistrust the check when it does not behave as promised. The corrected version asks less of the reader and delivers more: nothing about the checklist changes, only the reason for running it.
51-cross-asset-correlations.summary: The habit this lesson is trying to build is a genuinely good one: look at bonds, the dollar and volatility before you take an equity trade, and notice when your idea is at odds with what the rest of the market is doing. The pre-market checklist and the Confluence Matrix are the best expressions of it in the curriculum. But the lesson explained that habit with a mechanism that does not exist — that these markets warn you 12 to 48 hours in advance — and repeated it eight times, including in the SEO description, the case study, the quiz option, the quiz answer and the Key Takeaways. It also began at Part 2, having never written a Part 1.

52-volatility-trading.added: The single most practical thing the lesson was missing, given that its whole premise is reading VIX: VIX is quoted annualised, so divide by 16 for the implied daily move. VIX 16 is about 1% a day, VIX 30 about 1.9%, VIX 80 about 5%. That conversion does more work than the entire regime table, because it tells you directly how wide the stop has to be and therefore how many shares carry the same dollar risk.
fixed: Two hundred and sixty lines of after-record removed: Act 3's month-by-month Q3-Q4 table (+$32,900), Act 4's 2024 strategy-by-strategy table (+$112,200 across 128 trades), the before-and-after comparison table, 'Eric's Current Reality' with its $134K annualised pace, and the 'Total Impact of VIX Education' summary ending in 'ROI on VIX education: Infinite'. The Quick Wins and the practice exercise each carried a copy of the same figures; both cleaned. The disaster record stays in full, because it is arithmetically consistent and it is what teaches the lesson.

The dated VIX levels did not happen. 'Feb 24, 2023, VIX 29.4' — VIX was about 21.7 that day. 'May 4, 2023, VIX 24.3' — about 18.3. 'VIX hit 31 on Nov 3' 2023 — VIX was about 14.9, and it had not been near 31 at any point that autumn. Only the March 2023 credit-scare figure was close. All dates removed rather than corrected, per the pattern used elsewhere in this audit.

The lesson never mentioned that you cannot buy the VIX, then told the reader to trade its reversion. Added the mechanics that decide whether being right pays: every vehicle tracking VIX holds futures, and during a spike the front future already trades far below spot because the reversion is priced. And the trap in the lesson's own recommended expression — buying SPY calls during a spike is long delta AND long vega at the most expensive implied volatility of the cycle, so the vol crush works against the option while the direction works for it. Shares, or a call spread, express the same view without paying for the volatility you expect to fall.

'VIX > 30 reverts to 15-18 within 2-4 weeks' — contradicted by this lesson's own COVID case study, which correctly notes VIX stayed above 30 until early June 2020, fourteen weeks. 2008 held above 30 from September to April. Those are the episodes that make VIX spike in the first place and the ones that kill a reversion trade sized for a quick unwind. Corrected in the Key Takeaways, the practice exercise and the new Act 3.

The 'VIX < 15 = 75% size' row was presented as the same kind of rule as the others, but it runs the opposite way: low VIX means narrower ranges, so sizing off your stop already gives a larger share count for the same dollar risk. Relabelled as what it is — a discretionary tail-risk overlay, defensible but not implied by the volatility itself.

'Whale trades (10,000+ contracts) can predict directional moves 6-24 hours ahead' in the Key Takeaways — the same false lead-time claim corrected in Lessons 37 and 51. Replaced with what a large print does establish: dealers must hedge, which is real flow, and it happens immediately, not hours later.

'Checking one number prevents 30-50% of bad trades', 'trading high-VIX costs you 2-4x more per loss' generalised from 10 trades, 'Target 1: VIX return to 20 (usually +5-8% SPY move)' with its invented VIX-to-index conversion, 'one of the highest-probability mean reversion trades in markets', and the closing 'you just learned what separates professionals from amateurs'.
52-volatility-trading.kept: The disaster record and its arithmetic, the VIX regime table, the COVID case study (whose figures all check: VIX 12 to 82, SPY $340 to $220 for -35%, and buying above VIX 70 leaving you 35-40% higher six months on), the three quiz questions — whose gamma-pinning explanation is the best short account of dealer hedging in the curriculum — and the five-part practice exercise.
52-volatility-trading.notes: The only D so far, and the grade is for evidence rather than for the ideas. The lesson's teachable content would fit comfortably in a third of its length: size to the volatility, know what VIX 30 means in daily percent, understand why the reversion trade is usually expressed wrongly. What filled the rest was a fabricated career arc, presented in tables detailed enough to look audited — month names, trade counts, average R, running totals — which is precisely what makes it worse than a vague claim. A reader has no way to tell that a table is invented. Once it is gone, what remains is short, true, and enough.
52-volatility-trading.summary: More than half of this lesson was a performance record. Four acts of a composite trader's results ran from a half-year disaster through eighteen months of month-by-month P&L, a before-and-after comparison table, an annualised income figure and a 'total impact of VIX education' summary complete with an ROI line. Underneath all of that sits one genuinely good observation, fully supported by arithmetic that checks out: 62 trades in calm markets made $34,800 while 18 trades in fearful ones lost $52,400. That is $561 a trade against -$2,911 a trade, across 80 trades, and it is worth the whole lesson. Everything after it was invented.

fixes: Excised the 195-line after-record and replaced it with 'Phase 2: What She Changed -- and Why No Results Follow', which states the impossible premise, the double-count, the four changes worth copying, the IBKR Lite mistake, and what a disaster record can and cannot establish.

Rewrote the worked example so the limit rests on the bid, joining the queue rather than crossing it, and made the fill-rate/slippage trade-off explicit -- some of those orders never fill, and that is the actual trade being made.

Corrected the slippage ranges to a penny-spread baseline and added the retail-size line: at 200 shares of SPY the entire execution cost is one cent of spread and almost nothing else in the lesson applies.
Replaced the clock-based midday advice with the depth-and-urgency explanation and a journal exercise using real observed prices rather than an assumed multiple.
Fixed the Key Takeaways, Quick Wins and quiz so none of them still quote the removed improvement rates.
problems: Part 2 was 195 lines of invented performance record: Sarah's Q2-Q4 improvement, a before/after table, a full-year impact figure and a bottom-line ROI, all built on an impossible premise (65% win rate at +2.4R over 380 trades is roughly +912R a year).
The Q1 execution audit double-counted: the same trades were charged once as market-order entries and again as first-fifteen-minutes entries.

The worked 'limit order' example placed a buy limit at the ask. A buy limit at the offer executes immediately at the offer and pays the whole spread -- it is a market order with a different label, so the example demonstrated the opposite of its own point.

The recommended switch to IBKR Lite inverts the lesson's thesis: Lite routes to wholesalers for payment for order flow, so a trader whose entire diagnosis is execution quality gives up routing control to save a $117 commission line.
Slippage figures of $0.30-0.60 per share in SPY/QQQ were 30-60x the actual penny spread; the 0.1-0.5%-per-trade range quoted as typical describes illiquid instruments or oversized orders.
The midday-widening claim was false for liquid instruments -- the spread is a penny at 9:35 and a penny at noon; what is thin in the first fifteen minutes is depth, not spread.
strengths: Part 1's four-source decomposition of execution cost (spread, market impact, timing/delay, opportunity cost) is the clearest short treatment of the subject anywhere in the curriculum.

The central framing is exactly right and rarely stated this plainly: execution is charged on every trade, while edge only pays on the winners, so a cost that looks trivial per trade is not trivial per year.
The iceberg and participation-rate material gives a reader a concrete vocabulary for what a broker's algo menu is actually offering.
53-algorithmic-execution.title: Algorithmic Execution
53-algorithmic-execution.verdict: Part 1 is among the best material in the advanced tier and would grade A on its own. Part 2 was a fabricated performance record whose premise could not exist, and its two concrete recommendations -- the limit-at-the-ask example and the IBKR Lite switch -- both taught the reverse of the lesson's thesis. Repaired, but the lesson still leans on a single composite where a reader would be better served by measurements from their own fills.

fixes: Replaced Act 4 with what the two versions genuinely establish and what no version of the story can: the V1 gap is real evidence because it is a disaster, and one trader's fourteen months is roughly one market regime.

Added a callout naming the removed 'scales infinitely' claim and explaining why five retail systems are unlikely to be five independent edges -- most are momentum or mean reversion in different parameters, so running five correlated systems is running one at five times the size.

Rebuilt the transaction-cost section around checkable arithmetic: 200 shares of SPY, a penny each way plus commission, about $6 a round trip, and the rule that cost drag is cost per trade over gross edge per trade with trade count cancelling out.
Corrected the quiz answer and explanation to match, and rewrote the three Key Takeaways that stated the cost rule, the scaling claim and the Monte Carlo claim incorrectly.

Added the standard-error reading of the paper-trading table and stated the asymmetry plainly: a paper stage can refute a system and cannot confirm one. What it does confirm is that the rules are executable in real time.

Corrected the Act 2 look-ahead item -- fills were assumed at the signal bar's close, which is a bar of look-ahead rather than a slippage error -- and rewrote the practice exercise to report ranges rather than thresholds.
problems: Act 4 was an invented after-record -- fourteen months of live results, an income comparison table, a total-cost-of-education tally and a five-year projection of five systems at $50K each.

The lesson contradicted itself. The Real Talk box at the top says a system is capped by liquidity and by the capacity of the edge; the closing quote said 'systematic trading scales infinitely' and the comparison table listed scalability as 'Unlimited'.

The transaction-cost section was built on 0.08% of slippage per trade. On SPY that is 42 cents against a real spread of a penny -- roughly twenty times too high -- and the headline finding that costs take 29% of the edge was an artefact of that assumption.

The cost rule was stated backwards in the Key Takeaways and again in the quiz: costs do not scale with trade count relative to returns, because gross profit scales with trade count too. What decides the damage is cost per round trip over gross edge per round trip.
The paper-trading table read a 3-point gap on 50 trades as validation. The standard error there is about seven points, so the result could not have confirmed anything; it could only have refuted.

Monte Carlo was described as revealing 'true risk/reward distribution'. Reshuffling observed trades cannot say anything about returns that were never observed, which is the risk that actually ends systems.
The practice exercise set Sharpe > 1.0 on 200 trades as a threshold to clear, when a two-year Sharpe of 1.0 is consistent with a true Sharpe anywhere from about 0 to 2.
strengths: Part 1's framing is the best in the tier: every stage of the pipeline exists to kill the idea, and skipping a stage removes one of the ways it could have been killed. That single sentence reorganises how a reader thinks about validation.

The definition of a trading system -- rules complete enough that another person or a machine could execute them without asking a single question -- is exact, and the observation that most discretionary edges dissolve when written down is the honest reason most readers will fail at step one.

Tom's V1 disaster is genuinely evidential. A backtest at 78% and live trading at 48% on identical rules cannot be explained away, and the six-mistake breakdown maps each symptom to a specific process failure.
The walk-forward table gives a reader something concrete they rarely see: what an acceptable train-test gap actually looks like across several windows.
54-system-development.title: System Development
54-system-development.verdict: The strongest Part 1 in this stretch of the curriculum attached to a Part 2 that undermined it: a lesson about not fooling yourself with results ended with a five-year income projection. Repaired, it is now consistent front to back, and the cost-drag rule it teaches is one most published treatments of the subject get wrong.

fixes: Replaced Act 3 with what the two versions genuinely establish, plus a callout naming the residual overfitting in V2 and explaining what a forest score actually is.
Rewrote the confidence-threshold block: use the score as a ranking, re-check the cut-off on each retrain, and never trade the low scores in reverse.

Rewrote the feature section around the constraint that governs it -- pick three to six features, roughly ten trades per feature as a floor -- and turned the twenty-item list from a prescription into a menu.

Replaced the improvement target with a testable question: sort your logged trades by model score and compare the top third with the bottom third; indistinguishable outcomes mean stop, not add features.
Fixed the regime-score formula to a percentile-rank average with a note on why raw addition is wrong.

Rewrote the three Key Takeaways that stated the model-choice, feature-count and accuracy rules loosely, and replaced the closing flattery with the property the three failures share: each inflates a backtest invisibly from inside it.
Escaped a literal '<' inside the translated code blocks that was breaking the locked-term verifier's text extraction.
problems: Act 3 was an invented after-record: five months of live results, a baseline comparison claiming the filter added $21,300, a '62.5% improvement' headline, a journey table and a payback timeline.
The lesson praised V2 as the fix while V2 was still badly overparameterised by its own numbers -- 30 trees at depth 4 is roughly 450 split rules learned from 240 trades.
Random Forest scores were treated as calibrated probabilities throughout the threshold section. A forest score is a vote fraction; 0.65 does not mean a 65% chance.
The threshold table advised 'skip or inverse' below 0.45. Inverting a model's low-confidence output turns no information into a position that pays costs.
The practice exercise recommended 20+ features on 50-100 trades, which is the exact arithmetic the lesson blames for V1's collapse -- a direct self-contradiction with its own case study.
The exercise promised a 10-15% expectancy improvement, a target that invites tuning until it is hit and cannot be measured reliably at this sample size.
'Regime score: ADX + ATR + BB Width composite' adds three quantities in different units.
'Random Forest > Neural Networks' was stated as a law rather than as a consequence of sample size.
The paper-trading and walk-forward numbers were read as confirmation when the sample sizes only supported refutation.
strengths: Part 1 gets the framing right in a way almost no retail ML material does: the model is a filter over setups your method already produces, not a forecaster competing with institutions.

The three properties of market data -- non-stationarity, brutal signal-to-noise, and how easy leakage is -- are stated precisely, and the leakage point is exactly right: the resulting backtest is not optimistic, it is meaningless.
'Accuracy is the wrong objective' is the most valuable sentence in the lesson, and the 90%-at-0.3R example makes it concrete in one line.
V1's five mistakes are a genuinely good diagnostic checklist, each mapped to a mechanism rather than to a vibe.
55-machine-learning-trading.title: Machine Learning for Trading
55-machine-learning-trading.verdict: The best conceptual framing of ML in the curriculum, undermined by a practice exercise that told readers to do the exact thing the case study shows destroying an account, and by an invented recovery record. Repaired, the lesson is now consistent with itself: the V1 disaster carries the argument, and nothing after it is asked to.

fixes: Rewrote Michael's section around the split that matters: the depth term he caused versus the reaction to his sweep, with a procedure for separating the two on his own execution report. Removed the invented counterfactual and the quantified saving.

Replaced the PFOF composite with the arithmetic ceiling -- SPY's spread is a penny, so 2.3 cents is not a large number but an impossible one -- plus what PFOF genuinely costs (you never post, you do not choose the venue, the improvement benchmark is chosen at the instant of execution) and a fifty-fill measurement anyone can run.

Replaced the IEX case with what the speed bump does (protects resting orders from stale-quote arbitrage) and does not (nothing for orders you cross with, nothing for an order that never fills), plus why alternating order-by-order is the only version of that experiment that answers the question.
Corrected the latency-arbitrage mechanism and the front-running label, and explained why the distinction changes the defence.
Replaced the mental-stop advice with the stop-market versus stop-limit trade-off and the instruction to move your level off an obvious round number rather than abandoning the stop.

Rebuilt the worked example around the $80 spread ceiling on 8,000 shares, the crossing-versus-resting trade-off including fill risk, and a measurement worksheet, with the annualisation removed and named.
Updated the broker list (TD Ameritrade no longer exists separately) and pointed readers at the SEC-mandated quarterly PFOF disclosures, which are the one set of real numbers on the subject.
problems: Three separate composite savings records, all built on per-share figures larger than the instrument's entire spread: Sarah's 2.3 cents of PFOF slippage on SPY, David's 1.4 cents falling to 0.6 with IEX routing, and Michael's $0.85 average on NVDA.

Michael's case attributed the whole $12,750 to being front-run, when most of it was a 15,000-share market order walking past a top of book that holds a few hundred shares. The 'expected fill' of $410.50 was never available to an order that size.
It then quantified the counterfactual: a 12-minute iceberg 'would have' filled at $410.62, saving $10,950. That order never existed.
David's IEX experiment changed the routing at the same time as the month, three months running, and attributed the entire difference to the speed bump.
The lesson stated as fact that HFTs see your order before it reaches the exchange. Nothing sees an order in transit; what is visible is the print the first slice makes.
'Legal front-running' is the wrong term. Front-running is trading ahead of a customer order you owe a duty to; this is latency arbitrage.

The PFOF section claimed retail fills are 'always at ask (if buying)' and cost 1-3 cents a share, when wholesalers routinely fill inside the quote and the disclosed improvement is a fraction of a cent.
The playbook recommended replacing hard stops with mental stops -- advice that fails in exactly the conditions the flash-crash section describes, and that contradicts the rest of the curriculum.
The combined-tactics example annualised a single trade's $134 saving by 104 to reach $13,900.
strengths: The historical material is the most accurate in the tier and mostly checks out: the 2010 flash crash sequence, the ~20,000 busted trades at 60%+ away, Accenture at a penny, the August 2015 ETF dislocations, Virtu's 1,237-of-1,238 profitable days from the 2014 S-1, the Sarao and Tower Research cases with the right settlement figures and sentences.

The John Parker flash-crash example is the single best argument in the curriculum for understanding what a stop-market order actually is: filled at $88.50 with the ETF back at $104 an hour later, and never busted because 15.7% away was not 60% away.
The IEX explanation is genuinely clear -- 350 microseconds is the time a signal takes through 38 miles of coiled fiber, long enough that a quote change elsewhere arrives first.
The closing framing -- HFTs are fast but narrow, you are slow but can hold overnight and read context -- is fair and not flattering.
56-high-frequency-concepts.title: HFT Reality Check
56-high-frequency-concepts.verdict: The best-researched historical material in the advanced tier attached to three fabricated savings records whose per-share figures exceeded the spread of the instruments they described -- and a playbook item telling readers to abandon their stops. The corrected version now has a single organising insight that the original lacked: on a penny-wide instrument the spread cost is a penny, so any larger figure is your own order size, which is the one lever you fully control.

fixes: Replaced the backtest-becomes-live promise with what automation actually closes -- the gap between your strategy and your execution of it -- plus a callout listing every source of backtest-live difference it leaves untouched.

Removed Mike's recovery figures and replaced them with a reading of what each of the five controls prevents, and an explanation of why a recovery record could not establish that the controls work while the disaster establishes cleanly that their absence fails.

Rewrote the scalability example to say why the per-setup multiplication is wrong: $92 was measured on one instrument in one timeframe, and a setup ported to crude oil or gold should be expected to work less well, not equally well.
Replaced the setup-count claim and the uptime figure with statements that do not assert numbers nobody has.
Rewrote the opening so both sides of overnight automation appear: the winner you would have slept through and the loss you would have talked yourself out of are the same feature.
problems: Part 1 promised that 'your backtest performance becomes your live performance', which is false and is directly contradicted by Part 5 of the same lesson.
Mike's recovery carried a quantified after-record: $195K to $218K over eight months with 'no control ever failed to fire', repeated again in the quiz explanation.

The scalability example multiplied a $92-per-setup average measured on ES 15-minute out to five instruments and three timeframes to reach $9,600 a month, assuming without argument that an edge transfers across markets.
'Catch 50-200 setups/week' as the automated potential, in a table whose own footnote warns against counting correlated signals.
A precise-sounding 95% uptime figure for a home PC that nobody has measured.
The opening hook showed only the winning side of overnight automation.
strengths: The five-step translation framework -- entry, exit, size, management, filters -- is the clearest path from a discretionary rule to executable code anywhere in the curriculum, and each step names the specific vagueness a bot cannot accept.

The full bot implementation is unusually careful for teaching code: it excludes the current bar from the swing-low calculation (and says why the naive version can never fire), asks the broker rather than a local variable whether a position exists, uses a stable client_order_id so a lost reply cannot double the position, and reads environment variables rather than hardcoded keys.

The position-sizing section makes a point most risk material misses: a 2% risk rule says nothing about notional, and a tight stop quietly buys leverage. The notional cap and the recomputed real risk are shown side by side.
Mike's margin call is a clean disaster record whose arithmetic checks out at every step, and the failure has a single identifiable cause -- nothing in the code knew how much he already owned.
The correlated-symbols caveat is exactly right and rare: four correlated symbols firing at once is one trade at four times the size.
57-trading-automation-apis.title: Trading Automation & APIs
57-trading-automation-apis.verdict: The best practical engineering content in the tier -- the code is genuinely production-shaped and the commentary explains the traps rather than just avoiding them. What it lacked was consistency between its own promise and its own conclusion, and a recovery record it did not need. Repaired, it now says the same thing at the start as at the end: automation removes you as a source of error and nothing else.

fixes: Replaced the free-lunch claim with what the diversification benefit actually costs -- fewer of the best outcomes as well as fewer of the worst -- and pointed forward to Lauren's case as the same point with real numbers.

Rewrote the 60/40 risk decomposition to show the quick method, name why it is wrong, and then do the calculation properly, arriving at 93/7 and noting that the correct answer strengthens the section's own argument.
Renamed the inverse-volatility section and explained precisely how it differs from true risk parity and when the two coincide.

Added an estimation-instability callout to the efficient frontier covering noisy inputs, the sensitivity to expected returns, and the practitioner responses (weight constraints, shrinkage, dropping expected returns entirely).

Corrected the Kelly interpretation to a risk fraction per bet, added the parameter-uncertainty asymmetry that justifies fractional Kelly, and reconciled it explicitly with the 1-2% rule: use Kelly to rank strategies, not to set the level.

Rewrote the multi-strategy block to read the Kelly figures as ratios, to say what the arrangement does not buy, and to tell the reader to measure the correlation between their own strategies rather than assume it.
problems: Part 2 called diversification 'the only free lunch in finance', which the Lauren section then flatly contradicts.

The 60/40 risk decomposition squared weighted volatilities and ignored the correlation term -- the exact error Part 1 spends its length warning about. With the stated -0.30 correlation the true split is about 93/7, not 84/16.
The section labelled 'risk parity' was inverse-volatility weighting. True risk parity equalises the risk contributions computed from the full covariance matrix and generally has no closed form.

The efficient frontier was presented as something to pick a point on, with no mention that its inputs are estimated, that expected returns are both the hardest to estimate and the term the optimiser is most sensitive to, or that naive mean-variance optimisation produces unstable extreme weights.

Kelly's output was described as 'allocate 51% of capital', which reads as a position size. It is a risk fraction per bet -- 51% of the account lost on one losing trade -- and at 1-2% risk per trade this curriculum runs at roughly a fiftieth of it, a contradiction the lesson never acknowledged.
The multi-strategy table claimed three regime-matched strategies mean 'one strategy always working', which a slow directionless market falsifies.
strengths: Lauren's 2022 case is the strongest evidence in the advanced tier because every number in it is public and checkable: SPY -19%, EFA -25%, TLT -36%, GLD -9%, DBC +18%, VNQ -25% over Jan-Oct 2022, weighting out to exactly the -19.0% the table claims.

It runs the alternative allocation through the same window the trader actually lived, rather than through a flattering later year -- and then says outright that the tech book she abandoned beat the diversified one across 2023 and 2024, by a lot.

The TLT row is the best single teaching moment in the tier: the negative-correlation hedge lost 36% in the same year stocks lost 30%, and the portfolio still halved the loss, because seven sleeves driven by different forces did not all break at once.

'Diversification is not a return strategy, it is a survival strategy. Anyone who sells it to you as better returns AND less risk is selling you something' is the honest version of a claim almost every other treatment gets wrong.
The two-asset and 60/40 volatility calculations are arithmetically correct and verifiable line by line.
58-portfolio-theory-advanced.title: Portfolio Theory Reality
58-portfolio-theory-advanced.verdict: The best lesson in this stretch and one of the best in the curriculum. Its central case study is built from public data a reader can verify, it reports the cost of its own recommendation rather than hiding it, and its most memorable moment is a hedge that failed. The defects were technical rather than evidential -- a risk decomposition that ignored correlation in a lesson about correlation, and a Kelly interpretation that understated its own number by a factor of fifty -- and both are now corrected in place.

fixes: Removed the second half entirely and replaced it with what the first half establishes on its own, plus a note on why the $6,100 figure was not merely invented but methodologically wrong.

Added a selection-effect callout: attribution is far more reliable at telling you what to stop than what to double, because killing a clearly negative strategy is nearly free while doubling on six months of data is a real bet.
Corrected the Sortino claim with the arithmetic that makes it automatic, and gave the metric its genuine use -- comparing strategies whose volatility is shaped differently.
Added the Sharpe sampling-error paragraph and redirected the metric to within-sample comparisons where most of the noise cancels.
Rewrote the Quick Win to include beta, with worked cases at beta 1.0 and 0.5.
Added the allocation-versus-skill caution to the three breakdowns, with the fix: compute expectancy per trade alongside total P&L and record the trade count.
problems: Daniel's second half was an invented after-record: 153 trades, +$41,200, a month-by-month list, a full-year +$69,600, and an 'attribution value: +$6,100' headline computed by projecting H1's rate onto H2 and crediting the entire difference to the spreadsheet.

The lesson taught scaling the best-scoring strategy without naming the selection effect. Choosing the winner from three six-month samples is choosing the maximum of three noisy estimates, which is biased upward.

'Sortino > Sharpe = asymmetric returns (good!)' is wrong. Sortino exceeds Sharpe by construction for essentially any return series; a symmetric distribution produces a ratio of about 1.4, and Daniel's 3.0 against 2.0 is 1.5.

The Sharpe benchmark bands were presented without any sampling error. On one year of data the standard error on a measured Sharpe of 2.0 is roughly 1.0, which makes the bands wider than the differences between them.
The Quick Wins box defined alpha as return minus market return -- the exact error the quiz calls out two screens earlier.

The by-strategy, by-asset and by-quarter breakdowns used total P&L, which measures allocation as much as skill: two thirds of the return coming from SPY tells you nothing if two thirds of the trades were in SPY.
strengths: The central insight is genuinely valuable and rarely taught: an account total that is green every month can hide a strategy with clearly negative expectancy, and no amount of looking at the equity curve will show it.

Daniel's H1 attribution table is internally consistent to the dollar -- $48,900 minus $23,800 plus $3,300 is exactly the $28,400 the account made -- and the R-multiples, win rates and trade counts all reconcile.
The alpha section already carried the full CAPM version alongside the shortcut, and the quiz explanation correctly identifies subtracting the index return directly as the common error.

Several small-sample warnings were already in place and are well put: 20 breakout trades proves nothing, 8 trades in the lunch window is a hint rather than evidence, and the top-five winners are only identifiable afterwards.
59-performance-attribution.title: Performance Attribution
59-performance-attribution.verdict: The diagnostic half of this lesson is excellent and the arithmetic in it holds up. What it lacked was the statistical humility its own subject demands: it taught readers to find the best strategy in a small sample and scale it, without ever mentioning that the best of several noisy estimates is systematically flattering. Repaired, the lesson now says the useful thing, which is that attribution is a reliable tool for stopping and an unreliable one for doubling.

fixes: Retitled the lesson to 'What Actually Reduces a Trader's Bill' across the page, meta tags, catalogue JSON and the education index, and rewrote the Real Talk box and the closing to separate the tax from the saving, quoting the lesson's own numbers.
Added NIIT with its thresholds, its effect on both top rates, and why a trader with TTS is generally still inside it -- with a pointer to a CPA rather than a confident ruling.
Corrected the long-term rate presentation to 15% or 20% with the zero band's actual ceiling stated.
Added the market-risk cost of waiting for the long-term rate, with the symmetry made explicit: 17 points on $100,000 is $17,000, and so is a 17% adverse move.
Added the note that harvesting a loss does not require realising a gain, including the $3,000 ordinary-income offset and the indefinite carry-forward.
Flagged the mixed tax years in the scorecard and quantified the effect as a couple of hundred dollars.
problems: The title, the Real Talk box and the closing all promised '20-40%' -- conflating the tax burden with what optimisation recovers. The lesson's own worked example moves an effective rate 6.3 points, which is roughly a quarter of what the headline implies.

The Net Investment Income Tax was absent entirely. At 3.8% above $200K/$250K modified AGI it changes the top long-term rate from 20% to 23.8% and the top short-term rate from 37% to 40.8%, and trading gains generally fall inside it even with Trader Tax Status.
The long-term rate was given as '0-20%', with '$0-$20K' of tax on a $100K gain. The 0% band runs out around $47K of taxable income, so it is unreachable for anyone the lesson is addressing.
'Two extra days of holding = $17K saved' priced the tax and not the market risk of holding a large unrealised gain across two more sessions.
The tax-loss harvesting example sold the winners as well as the loser, creating a tax bill that harvesting does not require.
The scorecard mixes 2022 brackets in Column A with 2023 limits in Column B without flagging it.
strengths: Rachel's two-column comparison is arithmetically exact. The 2022 federal tax on $182,050 of taxable income stacks to $38,487.50 and the lesson says $38,488; the 2023 tax on $98,898 stacks to $17,135.50 and the lesson says $17,135; the Illinois figures apply the exemption correctly; every subtotal reconciles.

It kills the biggest myth in trader tax content outright: an S-Corp does not save a trader self-employment tax, because trading your own capital never generated any. What the entity does is manufacture earned income so a solo 401(k) can be funded at all.
It corrects the marginal-versus-effective error before doing any optimisation, and names it as the source of half the tax horror stories traders tell each other.
The Honest Scorecard reports the cash saving as $5,719 after the cost of the structure -- real but not life-changing -- and puts the retirement space in the row that actually matters.

The 'What This Case Study Is Not' box, the 31-days-flat cost of harvesting, the both-directions wash-sale window, and the 'ask your CPA before relying on this' note on substantially identical ETFs are all present and all correct.
60-tax-optimization.title: Tax Optimization
60-tax-optimization.verdict: The most careful lesson in the tier and the only one whose central case study reconciles to the dollar against the actual bracket tables. Its faults were a headline that promised four times what its own arithmetic delivers and one significant omitted tax. Both are fixed, and the lesson now says the same thing in its title, its opening and its conclusion: tax is 20-40% of your returns, optimisation recovers a slice of that, and the largest thing an entity buys you is not a lower rate but a retirement account you could not otherwise fund.

fixed: Removed the Q2-Q3 before/after performance table and the six-month $16,968-benefit / 7.7x ROI calculation, whose largest line was "losses I did not have" — unmeasurable by construction.

Removed the claim that fibre reduced average slippage from 0.08% to 0.03%: on SPY at $520 that is 42 cents a share, forty-two times the entire penny spread, and lesson 56's own latency numbers refute the causal story.
Added "What Actually Went Wrong" — all three failures identified as order-placement failures, with Disaster #1 shown to be impossible as written.

Rewrote all three prevention lists and the summary in cost order: submit the bracket on entry (free) before phone alerts, before the broker mobile app, before backup internet, before UPS/monitors/desktop.
Reframed backup internet as availability insurance rather than execution improvement.
Added a timeframe-keyed answer to "how much hardware do you actually need" — one good screen and a phone that buzzes for swing traders; screens do real work only when decisions are made in seconds.

Rewrote the ROI box, the key takeaway and the closing to state what the quarter does establish (execution failures are a nearly eliminable loss category, and most of the elimination is free) without a return multiple.
61-professional-infrastructure.notes: English plus all 11 locales rebuilt clean. Grade held at C: the disaster records are real and dated, but the lesson as shipped pointed every prescription at hardware, and its headline return figure was unmeasurable.
61-professional-infrastructure.summary: Three dated, mechanically-specific execution disasters carrying $5,559 of loss against $16,300 of gross profit — genuinely good raw material. The lesson then misattributes every one of them. All three were order-placement failures: a position with no resting order attached to it and a trader relying on being personally at a screen. Disaster #1 is internally contradictory as originally written — a stop resting at the exchange executes whether or not your router works, so the stop was never submitted, and no amount of backup internet addresses that. The page prescribed a hardware shopping list for a habit problem.

fixed: Replaced the Stage 3 gate 'Sharpe > 1.5 over 12 months' with a behavioural one, and added the reason: a twelve-month Sharpe carries a standard error of roughly 1.4, so a measured 1.5 and a measured 0.2 are the same reading.

Added a fourth column to the income-vs-capital table showing capital needed at 1% a month alongside the 2-3% assumption, and a callout arguing the 2-3% assumption deserves the same scrutiny the lesson already gives 8-10%: 2.5% a month compounds to 34% a year, net of costs, which almost no professional sustains over a decade.
Reworked the Quick Win formula to run at both 0.025 and 0.01, and framed the gap between the two answers as the size of the bet on an unearned return.
Flagged the same caveat in the key takeaways.
62-trading-career-path.notes: Evidence held at B only because Jason and Mike Chen are composites; everything they are used to demonstrate is arithmetic the reader can check, and the deposit split is the point of the case rather than a decoration on it. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
62-trading-career-path.summary: The strongest career lesson in the curriculum. Jason's 4.5-year record is internally consistent to the dollar and used against the reader's instinct: $148,500 of the $224,109 was salary he deposited, and the lesson says so in the section heading. It debunks the 90/90/90 statistic by name and replaces it with the ESMA broker disclosures, splits 'prop' into evaluation firms with simulated accounts and institutional desks that hire on resume, and prices a $10M fund's own audit and administration before calling $460K of revenue income. Two residual overclaims fixed.

fixed: Named and resolved a contradiction between the exit rule and the time stop: from |Z| = 2 the expected path is 1.0 after one half-life and 0.5 after two, so reaching Z = 0 takes about four and a half — meaning the 2x-half-life time stop fires before the exit rule on a pair that is working. Fix: exit at |Z| <= 0.5, which captures 1.5 sigma in two half-lives instead of 2 sigma in four and a half, roughly 60% more per unit of time and cheaper because friction is per round trip.

Explained why the 2-5% cap dominates Kelly rather than merely overriding it: p and b are estimated from a few dozen trades with a standard error around eight points, over-betting is punished far harder than under-betting, and the cap is roughly what quarter-Kelly gives once input uncertainty is taken seriously.
Added the cash benchmark to the Sharpe note: a market-neutral book holds collateral earning the cash rate, so the conservative tier's 6-10% total return is 2-6% of excess at a 4% cash rate.
Removed a duplicated "Quick Wins for Tomorrow" section that appeared twice on the page, folding its one distinct item into the surviving block.
Harmonised the half-life ceiling (was 20 days in Part 1.5, 5-30 days in Parts 6 and 9) and the Quick Wins stop threshold (was 3.0 against the conservative model's 3.5).
63-statistical-arbitrage.notes: Easy-to-get held at B: the lesson is genuinely demanding and assumes OLS, unit roots and AR(1) without teaching them, which is defensible at this tier. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
63-statistical-arbitrage.summary: Technically the most careful lesson in the advanced tier. It states the ADF null correctly and says explicitly that 1 minus the p-value is not the probability of cointegration; it prices the multiple-comparisons problem with real arithmetic (124,750 S&P pairs, ~6,000 passing on noise at the 5% level); and the intraday SPY/IWM example carries its own friction line, ending at +$2.20 net per trade rather than a percentage. The LTCM section identifies the correct failure mode — correlated spreads, not one spread moving too far. Four internal inconsistencies fixed.

fixed: Priced the lesson's own inversion rule against the episode it already admits was false: cutting equity 30-50% at end-July 2022 against SPY's ~45% total return to end-2024 versus ~10% for cash cost roughly fourteen points, plus two rounds of long-dated puts that expired worthless.

Replaced "when the curve re-steepens, go 100% cash or TLT" — the September 2024 dis-inversion produced no recession either, so the page's most aggressive instruction has now misfired on its most recent instance.

Stated the sample size plainly: about five clean post-war inversions, fewer still for re-steepening as an entry trigger, which cannot support a rule that moves a whole book. Rewrote the defensible version around the confirming indicators (PMI below 45, three months of rising unemployment, widening credit spreads).

Qualified the gold-in-stagflation claim: gold was legally fixed at $35/oz until August 1971, so much of the 1970s move was a one-time Bretton Woods repricing rather than an inflation response — a tailwind that cannot repeat, which makes "reliably" too strong for a claim resting on one decade.
Propagated both corrections to the quiz answer and the Quick Wins alert list, which had been repeating the unqualified rule.
64-macro-regime-framework.notes: Worth-the-time and delivers-promise held at B: the framework is sound and the history is accurate, but a four-box regime model with monthly rebalancing is a large amount of machinery for a retail reader, and the lesson is at its best where it costs its own advice rather than where it prescribes. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
64-macro-regime-framework.summary: The historical returns in this lesson are unusually well checked — the 1970s figures are real total returns and it correctly notes that the S&P's real price return was about -40% with dividends making up the difference; the 2022 numbers are right; the COVID and 2008 sequences are dated correctly. The problem was prescriptive, not factual: the lesson identified its own yield-curve false signal in 2022-24 and then left the trading rule that misfired on it standing unchanged, including an instruction to go 100% cash on re-steepening.

fixed: Removed the composite's six-month after-record (24 positions, $84M deployed, $47,300 of impact) and the $348,000 counterfactual saving it was used to compute — the saving is not observable, since it is the cost of orders that were never traded badly.

Replaced the invented "$2,111 impact cost" result with the square-root-law calculation that produces it: 20,000 TSLA shares against a 100M-share day at 3% daily volatility gives 0.042%, about $2,100 — a number the reader can check rather than a number they must believe.

Reconciled the opening $1M NVDA hook with the lesson's own later statement that megacap impact is measured in tens of basis points: 800K shares is a quarter of one percent of NVDA's day, and the square-root law puts the patient cost at about $155,000. The $1M is the price of sweeping the book in one go, not the price of size — which is the actual thesis of the lesson.
65-market-impact-models.notes: Easy-to-get held at B: the lesson is written for someone comfortable with participation rates and square-root scaling, which is appropriate here but is real work for the reader. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
65-market-impact-models.summary: Unusually strong on the mathematics and unusually honest about its limits: the Almgren-Chriss section flags that the worked example uses square-root rather than linear temporary impact and that the risk term's dollar level is a risk-aversion choice, not a measurement; the volume-curve table teaches the reader to read volume per unit time rather than share of day; and the multi-day example derives the 55% saving as 1 - 1/sqrt(n) rather than presenting it as a result. Two invented after-records removed and the opening hook reconciled with the lesson's own later correction.

fixed: Removed three quantified after-records attached to composite traders: Michael Torres's "+18.6% May 2023-March 2024" rebuild, Marcus's "8.5% over six months, roughly $4,800", and Amanda Park's "+$12,800 (+12.8%)" restart. All three describe trades that did not happen.

Replaced the Torres figure with the general point it was making — walk-forward optimisation makes a coarse trend rule survivable, not good, and any rebuild has to clear the benchmark of simply holding SPY, which returned roughly 26% in 2023 and 25% in 2024.

Replaced Marcus's realized result with what the redesign actually established (out-of-sample survival, parameter range, realistic costs) and kept the recovery arithmetic conditional: even at a full 18% a year, earning back $18,400 on $56,600 takes about twenty months.
Replaced Amanda's restart record with the observation that the gate which would have saved her was the cheapest one — two lines of multiplication before a dollar was committed.
Corrected a month-return: April's $7,800 loss is 11.0% of what was left after March, not 10.4%, which was $7,800 measured against the opening balance.
66-quantitative-strategy-design.notes: Easy-to-follow held at B for structure rather than prose: the lesson runs four separate composite disaster narratives plus an anonymous fifth, and they teach overlapping lessons. The arithmetic in each is sound and checkable, so none was cut, but the repetition is the weakest thing about an otherwise excellent lesson. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
66-quantitative-strategy-design.summary: Contains the single best passage in the curriculum: the Sarah practice exercise, where a strategy passes every robustness test in the lesson and is still rejected because SPY returned 10% a year over the same out-of-sample window and the strategy returned 4.3%. 'Robustness and profitability are separate questions, and the tests in Part 4 answer only the first one' is the sentence most trading education never writes. It also teaches the reader to compute a strategy's return ceiling from its exit rule before opening a backtest, and Amanda Park's cost arithmetic (19.0% of annual costs against a 19.8% backtest) is exact.

fixed: Replaced the unsupported "trade only above 70% confidence, win rate improves to 61%" with the two things that claim needs: a random forest's confidence is a vote fraction rather than a calibrated probability, and forests are overconfident near the extremes; and the filtered subset has to be measured on the test set with its row count reported, since a >70% threshold leaving 60 of 500 rows carries a 6-point standard error.

Added the same scepticism to the Sharpe column the lesson already applies to accuracy: those figures come from 500 daily bars each, where the standard error is roughly 0.7, so 1.3 and 1.1 are the same reading and neither is distinguishable from 0.4.
67-machine-learning-trading.notes: The composite after-records that survive here (Jason's rebuilt model, Michael Park's +5.4%) are all stated against the index they trailed, which is the deflationary direction the composite rule exists to protect; left in place deliberately. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
67-machine-learning-trading.summary: Opens by telling the reader that no model predicts next-day index direction above the 52-57% band and that an 85% backtest is a bug report, then names the three bugs. It teaches edge measured above the 50% floor rather than raw accuracy ratios, gives samples-per-feature >= 50 as the one number to carry, and diagnoses the Jason case precisely: not 'he only trained on QE' — the Fed hiked nine times inside his window — but that no dip in seven years had failed to recover. The 2007 Quant Quake framing (a backtest sees your positions, not the crowd standing in the trade beside you) is the best opening in the tier. One residual claim fixed.

fixed: Removed the composite's post-recovery record and its counterfactual saving ($195,000-$325,000 over six months of MEV protection), replacing it with the distinction that makes the section teach: the private RPC and the batch auction change the probability of being sandwiched, which nobody can score because the counterfactual has no transaction hash; the tolerance changes the size, and 5% on $400,000 versus 0.8% is arithmetic you can do before signing.

Converted the cross-exchange arbitrage Quick Win from an invented profit record ($28,600 in six months) into a costing of the same tactic: 0.5% gross on a $150 gap at $30,000 BTC, less 0.2% of taker fees on both legs, less withdrawal or pre-funding cost, less the spread actually crossed.

Made the MEV Quick Win consistent with Part 3: an average loss of $1,200-2,500 on a $50K swap is 2.4-5%, which means the trader's tolerance was set in that range, because the contract cannot settle worse than the number in that box.
Removed a duplicated "Quick Wins for Tomorrow" section, folding its one distinct item into the surviving block.
68-crypto-market-microstructure.summary: The sandwich section is the best explanation of MEV in any trading course I have read, because it gets the mechanism exactly right in both directions: the slippage tolerance is not a safety setting that protects you from bots, it is the number you hand the bots and they will take all of it; and a sandwich can never pay the bot more than it costs you, because the pool skims both of its legs on the way through. That second point is a working falsity test for every MEV story on the internet. The funding-rate annualisation (0.15% per 8 hours = 164% a year) and the May 2021 sequence are correct.

fixed: Retitled three sections that called composite examples 'Real Trader'.

Removed a nine-month success record (87 trades, 74% win rate, average win $1,180 against average loss $340, $180K to $247,700) and replaced it with the arithmetic that condemns it: that is a profit factor of 9.7 against lesson 66's own table, which puts a good profit factor at 1.5 and an excellent one above 2.0. A 74% win rate and a 3.5-to-1 payoff ratio do not co-occur, because the tight stop that produces the payoff ratio is what holds the win rate down.

Replaced Derek's counterfactual saving ($38,400 over five months from switching to icebergs) with the measurement a reader can actually make: pull your execution report, compute the difference between the price when you sent each order and your average fill, and the arithmetic on this page tells you what closing that gap is worth.
Trimmed the "saved $40K in 5 months" quotation to the part that survives.
69-institutional-order-types.notes: Delivers-promise and evidence held at B rather than raised: the mechanics are excellent, but the page still leans on the Marcus-versus-Aisha comparison, in which retail execution gives back 76% of gross profit — a figure that only holds in names where the trader's size is a meaningful share of volume, and that sits uneasily beside lesson 65's demonstration that megacap impact is tens of basis points. Left standing because it is explicitly a constructed comparison whose components are made to add. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
69-institutional-order-types.summary: Strong on mechanics — the stop versus stop-limit distinction, the Knight Capital timeline corrected to what actually happened (emergency financing five days later, Getco four months after, not a 48-hour collapse), and the iceberg display-size floor. But it carried the worst evidence problem in the tier: three composite traders under headings reading 'Real Trader', one of them a success story whose numbers fail the curriculum's own metrics test.

fixed: Removed the composite's counterfactual saving ("after using VWAP algos, saved $50K-$150K"), replacing it with the measurable version: her realised slippage per order, before and after, against the 0.1-0.3% band a well-configured algo targets.

Conditioned the "reduces slippage from 1.5% to 0.2%" headline, which the rest of the lesson spends its energy teaching the reader not to accept unqualified — on a megacap ticket neither figure applies.

Corrected the checklist entry "if algo buying accelerates (POV increasing), trend strengthening": a POV algo trades a fixed percentage of whatever is trading, so bigger slices mean the tape got busier, not that the institution turned bullish.

Harmonised the checklist's "when the algo stops, expect price reversion" with the corrected reading elsewhere on the page: it removes support, does not predict a reversal, and means nothing unless the algo was a real share of the tape.
70-execution-algorithms-twap-vwap.summary: Every worked example in this lesson states the order as a share of daily volume before it states it in dollars, and the exercises reward that habit: 450K COST shares is an 18%-of-a-day order and therefore a two-session job with a $700K-$1.4M impact budget from the square-root law, while 150K NVDA shares is 0.06% of a day and therefore not an impact problem at all. The 2018 opening disaster is internally consistent down to the LULD halt, and Exercise 2's VWAP arithmetic is exact. Two small defects fixed.

fixed: Applied the lesson's own independence rule to its own six-category confluence checklist. Trend alignment, moving-average alignment, RSI above 50 and MACD direction are four instruments reading one trend — in a strong move they agree essentially always, so ticking all four confirms nothing the first tick did not. Rewrote the scoring around the three genuinely independent inputs: direction, location and participation.
Corrected an arithmetic mismatch: 33 avoided stop-outs at the stated average loss of $1,080 is about $35,600, not the $25,600 quoted.
71-multi-timeframe-confluence.summary: Three passages carry this lesson. First: confluence buys you a cheap 'I was wrong', not a high hit rate — the value of stacked levels is that the invalidation is a single tight price, not that a bounce is likely. Second: the NVDA counterexample, where perfect EMA alignment across weekly, daily and 4-hour in July 2024 preceded a 27% fall in a month. Third: the closing line that multi-timeframe analysis works by subtraction and should cut your trade count more than it lifts your win rate — which Brian's numbers, internally consistent to the dollar, actually demonstrate. Two defects fixed.

fixed: Removed the composite's before-and-after profit framing ('-$8,400 + $34,050 = $25,650 after learning intermarket analysis') and the $300K position it rested on. The SPX path from 4,238 on 1 November to 4,719 on 15 December is real and checkable, and it stays; what one trader made from it is not observable and has gone.

Renamed the section from its dollar figure to what the case actually demonstrates, and added the two caveats: the signal missed the 27 October low by 121 points, about a fifth of the move, and the measurable benefit is the fourteen entries it would have prevented rather than the one it produced.
72-intermarket-analysis-advanced.summary: The October 2023 lead-lag walkthrough is the best-researched passage in the tier: every SPX close, DXY level and 10-year yield in the table is a real public print, and the lesson uses them to demolish its own field's favourite claim — copper was flat through the SPX low and gave ground in January while SPX kept going, so on that move copper did not lead, yields and credit did. It goes on to correct the Dow Theory record, the gold-versus-real-yields relationship (real yields were deeply negative through 2021 and gold finished down), and the folklore that credit always leads equities. One composite after-record fixed.

fixed: No content defects found. Retitled the long detailed action block, which shared a heading with the standard short closing block and rendered "Quick Wins for Tomorrow" twice on the page.
73-behavioral-finance-psychology.notes: The same duplicated heading was found and fixed in four other lessons by a repo-wide scan (39, 41, 65, 71). All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
73-behavioral-finance-psychology.summary: The strongest lesson in the curriculum on evidence handling. It cites the Brazilian day-trading study rather than folklore, caveats the Kahneman-Tversky 2:1 loss-aversion ratio as varying by person and context, names the Van Tharp '60/30/10' split as a number with no measurement behind it and keeps only the ordering, flags the Dunning-Kruger curve as partly a regression artefact, and gives the actual Dawson and Reid finding rather than the version usually quoted. The four-bias composite is built on real TSLA, GME and COIN closes from February to May 2021 — every date and price checks out, and the arithmetic ties to the dollar at nine separate points, ending at 77 times the loss his own plan called for.

fixed: Named the contradiction between the opening composite and the lesson's own Phase 3 success criterion: the criterion is 15-25% annually net of everything, and the example averaged 34.8% for four consecutive years with no losing year. Added a callout resolving it in the criterion's favour, cross-referenced to lesson 62's arithmetic on 34% a year.
Removed the composite's Sharpe track ("1.1 rising to 1.6" across four years), which is noise given a one-year Sharpe carries a standard error near 1.4.

Replaced the Sharpe gates in the capital-growth phases: 50-100 trades cannot distinguish a Sharpe of 1.0 from zero, and a twelve-month Sharpe is not much better, so Phase 1 now gates on expectancy and drawdown and Phase 2 on twelve months of profit plus a drawdown sat through without changing size.
Retitled the section away from its dollar figure, and pointed the reader at the two parts of the block that do not depend on how the market behaved: the cost line and the deposit split.
74-building-trading-business.notes: Evidence held at B because the year-by-year return path remains an invented sequence; it is now explicitly framed as optimistic and contradicted in place rather than presented as the expected outcome. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
74-building-trading-business.summary: The tax section is the most careful in the curriculum: an LLC on its own changes nothing about your tax, an S-Corp gives no relief from self-employment tax because capital gains were never subject to it, trader tax status is the thing that matters and has no statutory test, the 475 election is due in mid-April for a year you cannot see yet, and a $10,000 deduction at a 32% rate saves $3,200 rather than $10,000. Part 4's aside — a $150,000 account returning 20% makes $30,000, and you can draw a living from it or compound it, not both — is the honest sentence most career content omits. The four-year composite was the weak point.

fixed: Corrected the headline claim that the account fell $78,000, or -49%. It did not: about $8,000 was realised trading loss and roughly $70,000 was opportunity cost, and forgone gains do not come out of a balance. Added the general rule this exposes — a case study that adds opportunity cost to realised losses and reports the total as a drawdown is wrong in the direction that always flatters the story.

Removed the recovery's after-record ($82K to $137K, +67% in five months, 71% win rate), keeping the change that can be counted: 34 trades in the next five months against 8 in the previous five, on the same setups. Five months is not a sample, and quoting a return there would be doing the thing the corrected paragraph above it just took apart.
Trimmed the case-study heading and the trader quotation to match.
75-real-time-market-analysis.summary: A capstone that mostly earns the name. It states its own honest limit in the learning objectives — synthesising several streams buys context and a veto, not a measurable percentage — and repeats that discipline in each Quick Win ('what it gives you is a written reason to pass'). The quiz explanations are the best in the tier, especially question 2: three green pre-market numbers read as agreement is exactly the trap, because a genuine risk-on rally has bonds falling. Tyler's case had two arithmetic problems, now fixed.

fixed: Clarified the one ambiguous number in the confirmation checklist: "2.3x average volume (150M vs 65M avg)" compared a fifteen-minute breakout candle against a daily average, and SPY does not trade 150 million shares in a quarter of an hour. The bar is now stated as the breakout candle against the median volume of that same fifteen-minute slot over the last twenty sessions, with the session total kept as a separate check.
76-live-trading-case-studies.notes: The Maya after-record (47% to 73% over three months) is left standing because the lesson deflates it in place twice, naming both the sample size and the market's share of the change. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
76-live-trading-case-studies.summary: Four worked trades including a loss, each with sizing, management and a post-mortem, and the R-multiple arithmetic ties in every one. The best passage is the Maya section, which does what almost no trading content does: it says that scoring a pattern on the winners you selected it from tells you nothing, then re-scores all 218 trades by pattern so each carries its full record — and still calls 17, 12 and 14 trades small samples. The quiz answers are unusually careful (a dark pool print establishes size but not intent; volume is contemporaneous with price rather than lagging), and the takeaways state twice that no honest failure rate exists for the multi-timeframe check.

fixed: Gave the Jenna case the same treatment the Emma case already had: 33 trades carries a standard error on the win rate of about eight points, six months is one regime, and the market gets a vote in any six-month figure. What the style change demonstrably bought her is not in the P&L — it is the first stretch she finished without overriding her own rules.
Qualified the "Sharpe ratio > 1.0" pass criterion in the validation framework: a Sharpe estimated from two years of data carries a standard error around 1.0, so it is a floor and never a ranking.
77-building-your-edge.summary: The three-dimension frame is the right one and the verdicts on it are honest: informational edge is bought with infrastructure you do not have, analytical edge is where retail can compete, behavioural edge costs nothing. The Emma case is a model of how to present a discovered edge — it names the selection effect out loud ('a number found by picking out the setup that had already worked, which is exactly why the next six months are the part that counts') and then refuses to annualise the six months that follow. Tom's case correctly attributes his loss to latency, missed exits and revenge trades rather than to the strategy. Two smaller items brought into line.

fixed: Corrected the strategy description: credit spreads and iron condors are defined-risk structures, not "undefined risk". Every position he held had a capped maximum loss, which is what makes the case worth reading — he lost half an account without a single undefined-risk trade in it.

Re-diagnosed the failure by division. $143,000 across 18 positions is about $7,900 of maximum loss each on a $285,000 account, or 2.8% per position; eighteen open at once is 50% of the account at simultaneous maximum loss, which is exactly the -50% he took, because in a correlated crash every short SPY structure resolves the same way at the same time. That is a Layer 2 failure, not a Layer 1 one — each trade was sized like a professional, the book was not.

Reordered the "what went wrong" list to put the aggregate heat limit first, and noted that fixing the VIX filter, the daily loss cap, the circuit breaker and the size reduction without fixing that one would have reduced this loss rather than prevented it.

Removed the recovery after-record ($142K to $267K, +88% over 18 months) and replaced it with the bound the rules actually give you, which is checkable in advance: the same eighteen positions under a 5% aggregate heat limit cap the crash at $14,250 rather than $143,000. Also noted that the eighteen months after March 2020 were among the friendliest ever recorded for selling equity premium.
78-professional-risk-systems.summary: The five-layer stack is the right structure and the layers are genuinely distinct: per-trade risk, aggregate heat, daily circuit breaker, drawdown threshold, tail protection. Brian's case is the best material in the lesson once the arithmetic is done on it, and doing that arithmetic turned out to change what the case teaches.

fixed: Corrected the Tesla inclusion case, which claimed the stock "did not make a new high after inclusion". It did: TSLA closed 2020 at $705, took out the 18 December high on the last day of the year, and ran to roughly $880 by late January. Added what that means for the takeaway — the sell-the-news dip was real and brief, and a reader treating inclusion day as the top would have shorted into a further 27%. The reliable part of the pattern is the run-up between announcement and inclusion.

Corrected the merger-arb hedge. Shorting the acquirer hedges a stock-for-stock deal, where you receive shares and want to lock the ratio; MSFT/ATVI was all cash, and in an all-cash deal there is nothing to short. The arb desk's advantage there is position sizing against an estimated break probability, not a hedge.
79-institutional-trading-strategies.notes: Evidence held at B: the strategies are described accurately but several are presented as replicable at retail scale in more detail than the "what you cannot replicate" section later walks back. All 11 locales rebuilt clean.
79-institutional-trading-strategies.summary: The MSFT/ATVI merger-arb walkthrough is exact — announcement price, the widening through the FTC suit and the CMA block, the restructuring and the October 2023 close all check out, and both annualised returns compute correctly. The dark-pool section corrects the number most trading content gets wrong (40-50% of volume trades off-exchange, but true dark pools are nearer 10-15%; the rest is retail internalisation). Two factual errors fixed.

fixed: Removed the "EVERY month green for 12+ months" precondition and its two repetitions. A strategy running a profit factor of 1.5 produces losing months routinely — that is what a profit factor of 1.5 means — so demanding twelve consecutive green months selects for a lucky year rather than a durable edge, and it is the criterion most likely to keep a ready trader waiting or push an unready one into massaging the record. The lesson contradicted itself on this: its own case study attributes Amy's months nine and ten to variance. The bar is now twelve months of aggregate profit over a documented sample of 300+ trades, with the losing months visible in it.
80-career-pathways-trading.summary: The most honest career lesson in the curriculum. It replaces the '95% fail' folklore with the Brazilian and Taiwanese research and says why the research is more damning than the round number; it names the prop-firm incentive problem out loud (the firm earns on failed evaluations) and tells the reader to plan on being in the long tail; and its income table ends on the sentence the genre never writes — the returns are a function of account size, not skill, and a brilliant 30% year on $50,000 is $15,000. One internal contradiction fixed.
